title: Warm-Start Quantum Computation for Energy Readout and State Preparation
summary:
Estimating a ground-state energy and preparing a ground state both split into a front-end that supplies an approximate state $|χ\rangle$ and a back-end that reads or refines it. We argue, and measure at every step, that the only thing crossing that split is the front-end's spectral weight distribution $p_n=|\langle E_n|χ\rangle|^2$ over the eigenstates of the problem Hamiltonian $H_P$. Everything downstream is priced in it, so the front-end is a swappable module, and we swap it seven times without altering anything to its right. We call the arrangement WARP.
  Four back-ends spend that distribution. A readout (A) samples $g(t)=\langleχ|e^{-iH_Pt}|χ\rangle$ on the device and extracts true eigenvalues by classical signal processing, returning an energy below the variational bound of the state it was handed, from a signal $50\times$ shorter than a Fourier transform needs. Three routes spend the same account on a state instead. An adiabatic schedule (B) has a minimum gap set by the overlap; a discrete amplification (C) is cheaper in depth but must halt at an index the overlap fixes, so it needs a measured value and not a bound; a recursion (D) of depth $\mathcal{O}(3^m)$ raises the question of whether it can be run at all.
  The interactions are the substance. On stretched N$_2$ a sample-based diagonalisation reports a variational bound 79 mHa high, fifty times outside chemical accuracy; reading the state it has already prepared returns $E_0$ to $1.4\times10^{-6}$ Ha, three orders of magnitude inside it, and needs no new front-end and no new circuit. And because the weights price everything, they must be measurable when scarce, so we beat a weak reference against a strong one and recover overlaps four orders of magnitude below the shot-noise floor. We map the operating envelope throughout, and state the limitations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WARP, a modular framework that separates quantum algorithms into a front-end preparing an approximate state and a swappable back-end consuming its spectral weight distribution, demonstrating improvements in energy estimation across seven front-end swaps and four back-end variants.
AI.motivation: Estimating ground-state energy and preparing ground states are typically treated as monolithic tasks. The authors argue that the only interface between state preparation and downstream processing is the spectral weight distribution, enabling a modular, swappable architecture.
AI.method: WARP divides the pipeline into a front-end supplying approximate state |χ⟩ and a back-end reading or refining it, with the spectral weight distribution p_n as the sole interface. Four back-ends are studied: (A) a readout sampling g(t) with classical signal processing from a 50× shorter signal than a Fourier transform needs; (B) an adiabatic schedule with gap set by overlap; (C) discrete amplification needing a measured overlap value; and (D) a depth-O(3^m) recursion.
AI.result: On stretched N₂, sample-based diagonalisation reports a variational bound 79 mHa high (50× outside chemical accuracy), while reading the already-prepared state returns E₀ to 1.4×10⁻⁶ Ha, three orders of magnitude inside chemical accuracy, with no new front-end or circuit. Overlaps four orders of magnitude below the shot-noise floor are recovered.
AI.conclusion: The spectral weight distribution prices everything downstream, making the front-end a swappable module. The authors map the operating envelope and state limitations of each back-end.

title: Exact solutions of non-Markovian dissipative Ising models
summary: Applications of quantum devices and simulators require an accurate understanding of their dynamics as well as the effects of environmental noise. While some sources of noise can be modeled as Markovian dissipation, coupling to resonators or vibrational modes often produces non-Markovian dynamics as well, making it difficult to characterize the system, particularly for interacting many-body systems. Here, we identify a broad class of exactly solvable many-body quantum systems with both non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation. We consider a prototypical model of spins coupled to lossy bosonic modes that mediate Ising-type interactions. We exclude a transverse field but allow local spin dissipation that need not commute with the interactions, including dephasing, relaxation, pumping, and even processes that generate coherences. Using an exact stochastic representation, we decouple the many-body dynamics into the evolution of individual spins, yielding exact spin observables and correlations without adiabatically eliminating the bosons. In the Markovian limit, our solutions describe Ising models with correlated dephasing and nonreciprocal interactions. An example of spin squeezing shows that both the achievable squeezing and its optimal preparation time depend strongly on the interplay between non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a broad class of exactly solvable many-body quantum systems exhibiting both non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation, providing exact spin observables and correlations via a stochastic representation.
AI.motivation: Quantum devices and simulators require accurate understanding of their dynamics and environmental noise effects, but non-Markovian dynamics from coupling to resonators or vibrational modes makes characterization difficult, especially for interacting many-body systems.
AI.method: Using an exact stochastic representation, the authors decouple many-body dynamics into individual spin evolution, without adiabatically eliminating the bosons, for a prototypical model of spins coupled to lossy bosonic modes mediating Ising-type interactions.
AI.result: Exact spin observables and correlations are obtained; in the Markovian limit the solutions describe Ising models with correlated dephasing and nonreciprocal interactions, and a spin squeezing example shows achievable squeezing and optimal preparation time depend strongly on the non-Markovian/Markovian interplay.
AI.conclusion: The work provides exactly solvable many-body quantum systems bridging non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation, enabling exact treatment of complex noise effects relevant to quantum device characterization.

title: Engineering Ergodicity-Breaking and Stable Emergent Conservation Laws in a Generic Quantum Many-body System Under Strong Periodic Drive
summary: A periodically driven quantum many-body system is believed to approach a locally infinite-temperature-like state as dictated by the ergodicity hypothesis, when all the couplings/parameters are of the same order. When the drive is stronger than a threshold value, a large class of systems is shown to break this mandate, exhibiting Dynamical Freezing (DF): ergodicity is broken due to the emergence of local operators with permanent memory of their initial values (PRX 11, 021008, 2021). However, an exception to DF has recently been noted in a particular setting (PRX 16, 011041, 2026). Here we identify the condition for ergodicity-breaking in a system under strong drive, and show how to stabilize DF by exact, local engineering. We further show that the Floquet Hamiltonian $H_{eff} = (i/T)\ln{[U(T)]}$ is non-local when ordered by spin-flips, in a non-DF system, while it turns quasi-local under our simple, local DF engineering that keeps the Hamiltonian $H(t)$ still non-integrable at each $t$. This perplexing non-universality is absent in equilibrium, where non-integrability is believed to imply ergodicity and thermalization universally. Our work paves a way to engineering novel ergodicity-broken interacting Floquet phases of matter in various quantum platforms, and also endows DF-assisted quantum error mitigation and state stabilization techniques (see Nature 653, 1027 (2026)) with unprecedented versatility and flexibility.

AI.tldr: This work identifies the condition for ergodicity-breaking (Dynamical Freezing, DF) in strongly driven quantum many-body systems and shows DF can be stabilized via exact local engineering, revealing non-universality of Floquet dynamics absent in equilibrium.
AI.motivation: Periodically driven many-body systems are expected to thermalize to an infinite-temperature-like state by ergodicity. Strong drives can instead induce Dynamical Freezing (DF), breaking ergodicity, but an exception to DF was recently reported, so the precise condition governing ergodicity-breaking is unclear.
AI.method: The authors identify the condition for ergodicity-breaking under strong drive and design an exact, local engineering scheme to stabilize DF. They analyze the Floquet Hamiltonian H_eff = (i/T)ln[U(T)] in terms of locality when ordered by spin-flips, comparing a non-DF system (non-local H_eff) with the engineered DF system (quasi-local H_eff), while keeping H(t) non-integrable at each time.
AI.result: DF can be stabilized by local engineering; the Floquet Hamiltonian is non-local (ordered by spin-flips) in the non-DF system but becomes quasi-local under DF engineering, despite H(t) remaining non-integrable at every t. This demonstrates a perplexing non-universality absent in equilibrium, where non-integrability universally implies ergodicity and thermalization.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a route to engineering ergodicity-broken interacting Floquet phases of matter across quantum platforms and enhances the versatility of DF-assisted quantum error mitigation and state stabilization techniques.

title: TLS loss in superconducting resonators on epitaxial hBN thin films
summary: The integration of low-loss dielectrics into superconducting circuits is of importance to the functionality of quantum computers and sensors. In this work, we fabricate and measure niobium resonators atop few-layer, epitaxial hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy on a sapphire substrate and compare against a control counterpart without hBN. We conduct radiofrequency measurements which probe the responses to power, temperature, and temporal fluctuations of two-level systems. The resonators integrating hBN maintain low dielectric loss with a low-power internal loss tangent on the order of $10^{-6}$, and demonstrate hBN can be added to the conventional superconducting qubit stack with minimal degradation of the quality factor. This research represents a first step towards a materials-driven strategy to eliminate phonon-mediated correlated errors in solid-state quantum systems, which leverages the thermal properties of 2D materials to prevent athermal phonons excited in the device substrate from transmitting across the superconductor-substrate interface. The same technique applied to quantum sensors would maximize phonon collection by blocking phonons from entering passive metal films.

AI.tldr: Niobium resonators on MBE-grown few-layer epitaxial hBN/sapphire retain low dielectric loss (~10^-6 internal loss tangent), showing hBN can be integrated into superconducting qubit stacks with minimal quality-factor degradation.
AI.motivation: Integrating low-loss dielectrics into superconducting circuits is critical for quantum computers and sensors. The work aims to enable a materials-driven strategy to suppress phonon-mediated correlated errors in solid-state quantum systems by using 2D materials' thermal properties to block athermal phonons from crossing the superconductor-substrate interface.
AI.method: Fabricate and measure Nb resonators on few-layer epitaxial hBN grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy on sapphire, compared with a control without hBN. Perform radiofrequency measurements probing responses to power, temperature, and temporal fluctuations of two-level systems (TLS).
AI.result: Resonators with hBN maintain low dielectric loss with a low-power internal loss tangent on the order of 10^-6; hBN can be added to the conventional superconducting qubit stack with minimal degradation of the quality factor.
AI.conclusion: This is a first step toward a materials-driven approach to eliminate phonon-mediated correlated errors in solid-state quantum systems, leveraging 2D material thermal properties to block athermal phonon transmission across the superconductor-substrate interface; the same technique could improve quantum sensors by maximizing phonon collection via blocking phonons from entering passive metal films.

title: The Stone-Wales trefoil: a new topological defect in graphene
summary: Specific heat of graphite at high temperatures demonstrates significant deviation from the ``3R'' Dulong-Petite law. It can be explained by accumulation of defects with formation energy as low as 1.45 eV. Based on the density functional theory calculations, we propose a possible candidate of topological defects, whose energy is comparable to the growth activation energy.

AI.tldr: Graphite's high-temperature specific heat deviates from the 3R Dulong-Petit law; DFT calculations attribute this to the accumulation of low-formation-energy (1.45 eV) topological defects.
AI.motivation: The anomalously high specific heat of graphite at elevated temperatures exceeds the 3R Dulong-Petit limit and lacks a satisfactory microscopic explanation.
AI.method: Analysis of specific heat deviation and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to identify a candidate topological defect with formation energy comparable to the growth activation energy.
AI.result: A topological defect with a formation energy as low as 1.45 eV is proposed, whose energy matches the growth activation energy.
AI.conclusion: Excess specific heat of graphite at high temperatures is explained by accumulation of low-energy topological defects.

title: Correlated Pair Creation with Positive- and Negative-Frequency Oscillators in a Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulator
summary: Spin-dependent forces enable independent control over the effective frequencies of bosonic motional modes and their coupling strengths to spins in trapped-ion spin-boson quantum simulators. We show that the relative signs of these effective frequencies provide an important programmable resource for engineering distinct multimode dynamics. Focusing on a two-mode quantum Rabi model, changing the frequencies of the two modes from the same sign to opposite signs reorganizes the resonance structure of the spin-mediated bosonic interaction, converting the dominant resonant process from excitation exchange to correlated pair creation. In the dispersive regime, the resulting effective interaction realizes a two-mode parametric amplifier with stable oscillatory, critical, and exponentially amplifying regimes separated by a spin-dependent instability threshold. Across these regimes, the dynamics generate collective-quadrature squeezing and bipartite motional entanglement. Preparing the spin in a coherent superposition further allows different spin components to experience distinct stability regimes, generating tripartite spin-boson entanglement, while spin postselection can coherently combine the conditional bosonic branches to generate non-Gaussian entangled bosonic states. Finally, we outline an implementation using parameters within reach of current trapped-ion platforms.

AI.tldr: The relative signs of spin-dependent effective frequencies of bosonic motional modes are shown to be a programmable resource: flipping one mode's sign in a two-mode quantum Rabi model converts excitation exchange into correlated pair creation, yielding a two-mode parametric amplifier with stable/critical/exponentially amplifying regimes that generate squeezing, bipartite and tripartite entanglement, and non-Gaussian states.
AI.motivation: In trapped-ion spin-boson quantum simulators, spin-dependent forces independently control the effective frequencies of bosonic motional modes and their spin couplings. However, the role of the relative signs of these effective frequencies as a controllable resource for engineering distinct multimode dynamics has not been exploited. The authors aim to show that these signs provide a programmable knob for reorganizing spin-mediated bosonic interactions and accessing qualitatively new dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze a two-mode quantum Rabi model in which spin-dependent forces set the effective frequencies of two bosonic modes and their coupling to the spin. They vary the relative signs of the two mode frequencies and track how the resonance structure of the spin-mediated bosonic interaction is reorganized, focusing on the dominant resonant process. In the dispersive regime they derive the resulting effective interaction, which takes the form of a two-mode parametric amplifier, and characterize its stability regimes (stable oscillatory, critical, exponentially amplifying) separated by a spin-dependent instability threshold. They then examine the generated dynamics—quadrature squeezing, bipartite motional entanglement—and introduce spin preparation in a coherent superposition to let different spin components access distinct stability regimes, producing tripartite spin-boson entanglement, with spin postselection combining conditional bosonic branches into non-Gaussian entangled bosonic states. An implementation is outlined with parameters within reach of current trapped-ion platforms.
AI.result: Changing the two mode frequencies from the same sign to opposite signs reorganizes the resonance structure, converting the dominant resonant process from excitation exchange to correlated pair creation. In the dispersive regime the effective interaction realizes a two-mode parametric amplifier exhibiting stable oscillatory, critical, and exponentially amplifying regimes separated by a spin-dependent instability threshold. Across these regimes the dynamics generate collective-quadrature squeezing and bipartite motional entanglement. Coherent spin superposition makes different spin components experience distinct stability regimes, generating tripartite spin-boson entanglement, while spin postselection coherently combines the conditional bosonic branches to produce non-Gaussian entangled bosonic states.
AI.conclusion: The relative signs of spin-dependent effective mode frequencies constitute a programmable resource for engineering multimode spin-boson dynamics, enabling control over resonant processes, parametric amplification regimes, squeezing and multipartite entanglement, and non-Gaussian state generation. The scheme is implementable with parameters within reach of current trapped-ion platforms.

title: Percolation of Data Constraints and Reorganization of Boolean Function States in Parity Learning
summary: We study how a neural network reorganizes its learned function as training proceeds and as previously unseen parity data accumulate. The trained model is itself a Boolean function on binary strings of finite length. We then evaluate it on all data, inside and outside the training set, and read off its complete sign table. Its $\pm1$ entries are the amplitudes of a normalized state, dubbed the function-state, whose inverse subsystem purity $K_f=1/\textrm{Tr}(ρ_A^2)$ is an effective Schmidt rank. We find that small data additions broaden the Schmidt spectrum, whereas larger additions reconcentrate it in the target mode. The former is called differentiation because the model distinguishes inputs more sharply. The latter is called target-selective recoherence, where the model settles on the single rule shared by the added data. As the dataset grows, the connectivity of the constraint graph defined by the training set increases monotonically, whereas the learned inverse purity changes nonmonotonically. On a fixed connected dataset, as learning proceeds, the Schmidt spectrum begins to reorganize, followed by gains in target alignment and later by improvement in predictive accuracy. This ordering distinguishes three aspects of learning: constraint identifiability, function-state organization, and predictive accuracy. At fixed data size, a function that has already been learned can re-differentiate, an event we call retreat, without changing graph connectivity. Recovery reconcentrates the Schmidt spectrum in a similar target-selective pattern, without exact recurrence of the Boolean state. Thus the percolation of data constraints fixes the identifiable support, while the reduced state produced by training continues to reorganize even after that support stops changing.

AI.tldr: A neural network's learned function is treated as a quantum-like "function-state" whose inverse subsystem purity (an effective Schmidt rank) reveals that learning proceeds through differentiation and target-selective recoherence, ordering constraint identifiability, state organization, and predictive accuracy.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to understand how a neural network reorganizes its learned function during training and as new parity data accumulate, aiming to characterize the structure of learning beyond mere accuracy by examining the model as a Boolean function and describing its evolution through an information-theoretic/quantum-inspired lens.
AI.method: The trained Boolean-function model is evaluated on all inputs inside and outside the training set to read off its complete sign table; the ±1 entries form amplitudes of a normalized "function-state." The inverse subsystem purity K_f = 1/Tr(ρ_A²), serving as an effective Schmidt rank, is computed. The constraint graph defined by the training set and its monotonic connectivity are analyzed alongside the nonmonotonic learned inverse purity.
AI.result: Small data additions broaden the Schmidt spectrum (differentiation, sharper input distinction), while larger additions reconcentrate it in the target mode (target-selective recoherence, settling on the shared rule). As dataset grows, constraint-graph connectivity increases monotonically while learned inverse purity changes nonmonotonically. On a fixed connected dataset, learning orders itself: Schmidt spectrum reorganization, then target alignment gains, then predictive-accuracy improvement. A learned function can "retreat" (re-differentiate at fixed data size) without changing graph connectivity; recovery reconcentrates the spectrum in a similar target-selective pattern without exact Boolean-state recurrence.
AI.conclusion: Percolation of data constraints fixes the identifiable support, whereas the reduced state produced by training continues to reorganize even after that support stops changing. This distinguishes three aspects of learning: constraint identifiability, function-state organization, and predictive accuracy.

title: Error correction and quantum information spreading on sparse random graphs
summary: Quantum error-correcting codes on graph geometries beyond regular euclidean lattices have emerged as a promising route toward robust quantum information processing. A major challenge in quantum error correction is the trade-off between favorable properties of codes constructed in high dimensionality and the need for locality in practical implementations on near-term hardware. Sparse intermediate geometries may combine the advantages of both, but how their structure governs quantum information dynamics and code performance remains unclear. Here we show that the spectral dimension $d_s$, defined from the low-energy spectrum of the graph Laplacian, is the universal parameter connecting these properties. Using Floquet random Clifford circuits on two distinct sparse graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension, we find that $d_s$ governs both quantum information spreading and the scaling of the resulting quantum error-correcting code distance. We identify a geometry-induced entanglement phase transition from localized area-law to ergodic volume-law, whose universality is determined by $d_s$ and exhibits long-range percolation criticality. In the ergodic phase, the circuit acts as a CSS code encoder whose code distance is set by the competition between two logical sectors --- the cost of severing the graph and the length of its shortest winding cycle --- which connectivity pushes in opposite directions. The spectral dimension organizes this trade-off, highlighting a maximum at intermediate $d_s$ retaining sparse connectivity and physical realizability.

AI.tldr: The spectral dimension d_s of sparse graph geometries universally governs quantum information spreading and code distance in Floquet random Clifford circuits, revealing a geometry-induced entanglement phase transition and an optimal intermediate d_s maximizing code performance.
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correcting codes on graph geometries offer a route to robust quantum information processing, but there is a trade-off between the favorable properties of high-dimensional codes and the locality required for near-term hardware. Sparse intermediate geometries may combine both advantages, yet how their structure governs quantum information dynamics and code performance remained unclear.
AI.method: The authors employ Floquet random Clifford circuits on two distinct sparse graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension d_s, defined from the low-energy spectrum of the graph Laplacian, and analyze how d_s controls information spreading and the scaling of the code distance.
AI.result: The spectral dimension d_s governs both quantum information spreading and the scaling of the code distance. A geometry-induced entanglement phase transition from localized area-law to ergodic volume-law is identified, with universality set by d_s and exhibiting long-range percolation criticality. In the ergodic phase, the circuit acts as a CSS code encoder whose distance is set by the competition between the cost of severing the graph and the length of its shortest winding cycle, with connectivity pushing these in opposite directions. This trade-off is maximized at intermediate d_s.
AI.conclusion: The spectral dimension is the universal parameter organizing the trade-off between code properties and locality, with a maximum at intermediate d_s that retains sparse connectivity and physical realizability, highlighting sparse graph geometries as a practical design principle for quantum error-correcting codes.

title: Encoding Matters: A Qubit-Efficient Reformulation for Quantum Resilient Routing
summary: Qubits are powerful computational resources because each additional qubit doubles the size of the accessible state space. This expressive power comes at a cost: adding qubits also increases circuit size, constraint overhead, and exposure to hardware noise. These limitations are especially critical for near-term quantum computers, making the number of qubits required to formulate a problem a central practical concern. In this work, we present a method for efficiently mapping logistics and routing problems onto qubits through structure-aware encoding reduction. We demonstrate the method on a benchmark problem of latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures. For this benchmark, the reduced formulation substantially lowers both the qubit count and the compiled circuit complexity while preserving the original optimization task. By running the reduced model on the same trapped-ion quantum computer as the benchmark, we obtain a 100X improvement in the success probability. This finding shows how careful problem formulation can make current quantum hardware substantially more effective for practical optimization.

AI.tldr: Structure-aware encoding reduction lowers qubit count and circuit complexity for logistics/routing problems, yielding a 100X success-probability improvement on a trapped-ion quantum computer for latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures.
AI.motivation: Each added qubit doubles the accessible state space but also increases circuit size, constraint overhead, and hardware noise exposure. This trade-off is especially limiting for near-term quantum devices, making qubit-count minimization for problem formulation a central practical concern.
AI.method: The authors propose a structure-aware encoding-reduction method that maps logistics and routing problems onto qubits by exploiting problem structure to shrink the encoding. They demonstrate it on a benchmark of latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures, compiling and running both the reduced and original formulations on the same trapped-ion quantum computer.
AI.result: The reduced formulation substantially lowers both qubit count and compiled circuit complexity while preserving the original optimization task. On hardware, the reduced model achieves a 100X improvement in success probability over the benchmark formulation.
AI.conclusion: Careful, structure-aware problem formulation can make current quantum hardware substantially more effective for practical optimization, underscoring encoding reduction as a key lever for near-term quantum advantage in logistics and routing.

title: Dissipative Majorana Chain---Anomalies and Non-Invertible Symmetries
summary: We study symmetries and anomalies of dissipative Majorana chains described by Lindblad dynamics. Using the operator-state mapping, we represent the Lindbladian as a non-Hermitian operator on a doubled Hilbert space. In this formulation, the ket and bra contours admit strong fermion parities and strong translations, while their diagonal combinations define weak symmetries. For even and odd chain lengths, we diagnose anomalies by comparing symmetry algebras with and without weak fermion-parity defects. These algebras retain the lattice precursor of the modulo-$8$ anomaly of the closed Majorana chain and exhibit projective relations between strong fermion parity and weak translation, as well as between weak fermion parity and strong translation, which are intrinsic to open quantum systems. We establish the IR correspondence between the lattice symmetry algebras and those of the doubled Majorana CFT in four spin sectors, identifying chiral fermion parities emanated from the lattice translations. Finally, we develop the lattice bosonization of the dissipative chain. For even length with collective energy dephasing, combining the defect and no-defect sectors and imposing GSO projections gives rise to an Ising Lindbladian with non-invertible Kramers--Wannier symmetries descending from the anomalous strong translation and fermion parity of the Majorana chain. For odd length, constructing mutually commuting ket- and bra-sector spin operators instead yields an Ising Lindbladian with a Kramers--Wannier duality defect. Our results provide a controlled framework for extending lattice anomalies and non-invertible symmetries to open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies symmetries and anomalies of dissipative Majorana chains under Lindblad dynamics, using an operator-state mapping to doubled Hilbert space, and extends lattice anomalies and non-invertible symmetries to open quantum systems via lattice bosonization yielding Ising Lindbladians with Kramers–Wannier symmetries.
AI.motivation: Lattice anomalies and non-invertible symmetries are well understood in closed quantum systems, but their extension to open (dissipative) quantum systems remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to provide a controlled framework for transporting these concepts to Lindbladian dynamics.
AI.method: Using the operator-state mapping, the Lindbladian is represented as a non-Hermitian operator on a doubled Hilbert space, where ket and bra contours carry strong fermion parities and strong translations while diagonal combinations define weak symmetries. Anomalies are diagnosed by comparing symmetry algebras with and without weak fermion-parity defects for even and odd chain lengths, and lattice bosonization is developed, with GSO projections imposed.
AI.result: The symmetry algebras retain the lattice precursor of the modulo-8 anomaly of the closed Majorana chain and show projective relations between strong fermion parity and weak translation, and between weak fermion parity and strong translation. An IR correspondence is established between the lattice symmetry algebras and those of the doubled Majorana CFT in four spin sectors. For even length with collective energy dephasing, an Ising Lindbladian emerges with non-invertible Kramers–Wannier symmetries; for odd length, an Ising Lindbladian with a Kramers–Wannier duality defect is obtained.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a controlled framework for extending lattice anomalies and non-invertible symmetries to open quantum systems, revealing anomaly structures intrinsic to Lindblad dynamics such as projective relations between strong and weak symmetries.

title: Optimal linear-optical interferometers for unitary t-designs in a multi-photon Fock space
summary: We investigate the construction of unitary $t$-designs in a multi-photon Fock space on programmable linear-optical interferometers. Using the frame potential as the optimization objective, we identify architectures that realize approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs with considerably fewer controllable parameters than required for universal linear optics. For example, we find numerical evidence suggesting that for unitary 1-designs, the required number of programmable parameters scales empirically as $2d$ with the number of modes $d$, instead of $O(d^2)$. We benchmark the resulting ensembles using single-photon transition probabilities and average channel fidelities. Furthermore, as a practical result, we develop a photon-number estimation protocol for multi-photon Fock states that leverages these optimized 1- and 2-designs. Our findings demonstrate that shallow interferometers can accurately reproduce Haar-averaged first moments, while second-moment-sensitive observables provide a considerably stricter test for approximate unitary 2-designs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies construction of approximate unitary t-designs in multi-photon Fock spaces using programmable linear-optical interferometers, optimizing frame potential to find shallow architectures, and applies them to photon-number estimation.
AI.motivation: Universal linear optics requires O(d^2) controllable parameters, which is resource-intensive. The authors seek architectures that realize approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs with far fewer programmable parameters.
AI.method: Frame potential is used as the optimization objective to identify shallow interferometer architectures achieving approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs in multi-photon Fock space. Ensembles are benchmarked via single-photon transition probabilities and average channel fidelities, and a photon-number estimation protocol is developed based on the optimized designs.
AI.result: Numerical evidence suggests the required number of programmable parameters for unitary 1-designs scales empirically as 2d with mode number d, rather than O(d^2). Shallow interferometers reproduce Haar-averaged first moments accurately, while second-moment-sensitive observables provide a stricter test for approximate unitary 2-designs.
AI.conclusion: Shallow programmable interferometers can realize approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs with substantially fewer parameters than universal linear optics, and these designs enable practical photon-number estimation for multi-photon Fock states.

title: Latent Symmetry in Quantum Zeno Dynamics
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in Advanced Quantum Technologies
summary: Quantum Zeno dynamics constrains a continuously monitored system to measurement-selected subspaces. Here we show that the structure of such Zeno subspaces can be governed by a \emph{latent symmetry}, namely a symmetry that is absent from the geometry of the underlying physical network. We consider a minimal circuit-QED network of coupled microwave resonators subject to quantum-nondemolition (QND) monitoring of local photon occupations. Two distinguished resonators are geometrically inequivalent, yet are exactly exchanged by a latent symmetry of the network. Strong monitoring partitions the single-excitation Hilbert space into three quantum-Zeno subspaces, two of which correspond to localization on the distinguished resonators. Latent symmetry exactly exchanges these two Zeno subspaces and enforces identical escape and residence statistics despite their different microscopic environments. In the strong-measurement regime their residence times grow linearly with the measurement strength and diverge in the ideal Zeno limit, where the measurement subspaces become dynamically disconnected. Our results show that latent symmetry can act as a hidden organizing principle of quantum Zeno dynamics, imposing exact relations between measurement-selected subspaces that are geometrically inequivalent in the physical system.

AI.tldr: Latent symmetry—a symmetry absent from the physical network geometry—organizes quantum Zeno subspaces, exactly exchanging two geometrically inequivalent localization subspaces and enforcing identical escape and residence statistics, with residence times diverging in the ideal Zeno limit.
AI.motivation: Quantum Zeno dynamics confines a monitored system to measurement-selected subspaces, but the principles governing the structure of these Zeno subspaces are not well understood. The authors aim to show that latent symmetry, rather than physical network geometry, can serve as a hidden organizing principle for Zeno subspace structure.
AI.method: The authors study a minimal circuit-QED network of coupled microwave resonators under quantum-nondemolition (QND) monitoring of local photon occupations. Two geometrically inequivalent resonators are exactly exchanged by a latent symmetry of the network. Strong monitoring partitions the single-excitation Hilbert space into three quantum-Zeno subspaces, two of which correspond to localization on the distinguished resonators.
AI.result: Latent symmetry exactly exchanges the two localization Zeno subspaces and enforces identical escape and residence statistics despite their different microscopic environments. In the strong-measurement regime, residence times grow linearly with measurement strength and diverge in the ideal Zeno limit, where measurement subspaces become dynamically disconnected.
AI.conclusion: Latent symmetry can act as a hidden organizing principle of quantum Zeno dynamics, imposing exact relations between measurement-selected subspaces that are geometrically inequivalent in the physical system.

title: A Catalytic Algorithm for Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries with Tight Query Bounds
summary: We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary $U\in\mathrm{SU}(3)$ using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements $m$ transpositions or inversions with $3+4m$ or $3+8m$ total queries, respectively. More generally, we prove that exact transposition and inversion of an unknown $U\in\mathrm{SU}(d)$, $d\ge2$, require at least $d+1$ and $d^2-1$ processing queries, respectively, in fixed causal order. These processing bounds hold for any program state prepared independently of the input state using finitely many forward queries, even if that state is consumed during processing. Both our catalytic qutrit algorithms attain their respective bounds. Moreover, exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries requires at least three preparation queries, and our construction attains this bound.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs exact deterministic catalytic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary using forward queries only, and proves matching lower bounds on the number of queries required.
AI.motivation: Exact transposition and inversion of an unknown unitary are fundamental operations, but their query complexity under fixed causal order with forward-only queries is not fully characterized. The authors aim to determine optimal query counts and demonstrate that these bounds are attainable in the qutrit case.
AI.method: The authors design deterministic circuits for U in SU(3): three queries prepare a catalyst independent of the input state, four more queries implement transposition while preserving the catalyst, and two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries. They also prove general lower bounds on processing queries for SU(d) under fixed causal order for any program state prepared independently of the input.
AI.result: Transposition uses 4 processing queries and inversion uses 8, with total queries 3+4m or 3+8m for m operations. Lower bounds are d+1 processing queries for transposition and d^2-1 for inversion. The catalytic qutrit algorithms achieve these bounds, and exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries needs at least three preparation queries, which the construction meets.
AI.conclusion: Exact catalytic transposition and inversion of an unknown qutrit unitary are achievable with optimal query complexity: four and eight processing queries respectively, plus three preparation queries, and these match proven lower bounds for fixed causal order.

title: Fast computational primitives for La-cross qLDPC codes
summary: Quantum LDPC codes promise to reduce the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their practical use requires efficient logical gates, measurements, and access to non-Clifford resources. Here, we develop a complete set of computational primitives for La-cross hypergraph product codes. For a subclass of these codes, we show that seed automorphisms together with fold-transversal gates generate the full logical Clifford group up to Pauli corrections. We further prove that every rank one logical operator admits $D$ pairwise disjoint physical representatives, enabling parallel gauging and a space--time tradeoff for logical measurements. Finally, we construct an addressable surface code interface for injecting externally prepared resource states into selected logical qubits. Together, these results establish La-cross codes as a simple, low-connectivity generalisation of surface code computation, retaining analogous computational primitives while providing a complete Clifford+$T$ instruction set across multiple encoded qubits.

AI.tldr: This work develops a complete set of computational primitives for La-cross hypergraph product codes, covering logical Clifford gates, parallel logical measurements, and a surface code interface for non-Clifford resource-state injection.
AI.motivation: Quantum LDPC codes promise reduced fault-tolerant overhead, but practical use requires efficient logical gates, measurements, and access to non-Clifford resources.
AI.method: For La-cross hypergraph product codes, the authors combine seed automorphisms with fold-transversal gates; prove that rank-one logical operators admit D pairwise disjoint physical representatives; and construct an addressable surface code interface for injecting externally prepared resource states into selected logical qubits.
AI.result: For a subclass of these codes, seed automorphisms together with fold-transversal gates generate the full logical Clifford group up to Pauli corrections. The disjoint representatives enable parallel gauging and a space-time tradeoff for logical measurements. The interface supports injection of externally prepared resource states into selected logical qubits.
AI.conclusion: La-cross codes constitute a simple, low-connectivity generalization of surface code computation, retaining analogous computational primitives while providing a complete Clifford+T instruction set across multiple encoded qubits.

title: Coset Lifted Product Codes: Constructing Quantum LDPC Codes from Non-Normal Subgroup Actions
summary: We introduce coset lifted product (CLP) codes, a family of quantum LDPC codes that combine the protograph structure of lifted product codes with the coset action of Aydin, Tamo, and Barg \cite{AydinTamoBarg2026}. Given a finite group $G$, a subgroup $H \le G$ that need not be normal, a protograph $A$ over $\mathbb F_2[G]$, and a protograph $B$ over $\mathbb F_2[N_G(H)]$, the two protographs act on the cosets $G/H$ from the left and from the right to produce quantum CSS codes. Further, for groups of odd order, we give an explicit formula for the dimension as a sum over the irreducible representations $ρ$ of $G$ of hypergraph product dimensions. A search over $14,843$ pairs $(G,H)$ with $H$ restricted to be non-normal and $120 \le n \le 400$ yields certified codes that exceed the best published value of $Q=kd^2/n$ at check weights $6,7$ and $9$, i.e., we obtain $[[360,20,20]]$ at $w=6$, a $[[360,24,20]]$ code at $w=7$, and codes $[[252,16,18]]$ and $[[288,16,20]]$ at $w=9$. Our search also produce high-distance codes with parameters $[[168,10,14]], [[240,8,20]]$ at $w=6$ and $[[216,8,18]]$ at $w=7$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces coset lifted product (CLP) codes, a new family of quantum LDPC codes combining lifted product protographs with a coset action from Aydin, Tamo, and Barg, yielding explicit dimension formulas for odd-order groups and improved Q=kd^2/n codes at check weights 6, 7, and 9.
AI.motivation: Lifted product codes provide strong quantum LDPC constructions, but their framework has been limited to standard group-algebra protographs. The authors aim to generalize this by incorporating a coset action, enabling non-normal subgroups to act on cosets and thereby expanding the code design space to find codes with better parameters (notably higher Q=kd^2/n).
AI.method: Given a finite group G, a (possibly non-normal) subgroup H ≤ G, a protograph A over F_2[G], and a protograph B over F_2[N_G(H)], the two protographs act on the cosets G/H from the left and right to construct quantum CSS codes. For groups of odd order, an explicit dimension formula is derived as a sum over irreducible representations ρ of G of hypergraph product dimensions. A computational search over 14,843 pairs (G,H), with H restricted to non-normal and block length 120 ≤ n ≤ 400, is performed to find certified codes.
AI.result: The search yields certified codes exceeding the best published Q=kd^2/n at check weights 6, 7, and 9: [[360,20,20]] at w=6, [[360,24,20]] at w=7, and [[252,16,18]] and [[288,16,20]] at w=9. It also produces high-distance codes [[168,10,14]] and [[240,8,20]] at w=6, and [[216,8,18]] at w=7.
AI.conclusion: Coset lifted product codes generalize lifted product codes through a coset action, admit a tractable dimension formula for odd-order groups via irreducible representations, and empirically deliver state-of-the-art quantum LDPC codes with improved Q=kd^2/n at several check weights.

title: Analog quantum simulation of Shastry-Sutherland Ising materials
summary: Frustrated magnets host rich emergent behavior because competing interactions generate dense manifolds of low-energy states. The Ising Shastry-Sutherland model is a paradigmatic setting, motivated experimentally by Ising-like rare-earth tetraborides such as TmB$_4$ and ErB$_4$, whose field-induced magnetization plateaus have motivated extensive microscopic modeling. Yet how tunable quantum fluctuations reorganize this material-motivated phase diagram remains largely unexplored. Here, we realize a transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice using a programmable Rydberg-atom array. We map its quantum phase diagram using density matrix renormalization group calculations and probe corresponding signatures experimentally in arrays containing more than 110 atoms. Beyond the established classical phases, the calculations identify two regimes absent in the classical limit and stabilized at finite transverse field: a $2/5$ filling plateau whose finite stability region emerges from a classically degenerate phase boundary and a symmetry-preserving quantum-dimer regime replacing classically selected collinear order. Experiments on finite open arrays reveal signatures consistent with these regimes across three boundary-pinning conditions, with the resulting response maps agreeing qualitatively with the calculated phase diagram. Our results establish programmable Rydberg-atom arrays as tools for exploring frustrated, material-motivated Hamiltonians and motivate searches for new, quantum-driven magnetization plateaus and quantum-dimer behavior in ErB$_4$ under a transverse field or in strain-tuned TmB$_4$.

AI.tldr: Using a programmable Rydberg-atom array, the authors realize a transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, map its quantum phase diagram with DMRG, and observe signatures of two classically absent regimes: a 2/5 filling plateau and a symmetry-preserving quantum-dimer phase.
AI.motivation: The Ising Shastry-Sutherland model is experimentally motivated by Ising-like rare-earth tetraborides (TmB4, ErB4) with field-induced magnetization plateaus, but how tunable quantum fluctuations reorganize this material-motivated phase diagram remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Realize a transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice using a programmable Rydberg-atom array; map the quantum phase diagram via density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations; probe corresponding signatures experimentally in arrays containing more than 110 atoms across three boundary-pinning conditions.
AI.result: Beyond established classical phases, calculations identify two regimes absent in the classical limit and stabilized at finite transverse field: a 2/5 filling plateau whose finite stability region emerges from a classically degenerate phase boundary, and a symmetry-preserving quantum-dimer regime replacing classically selected collinear order. Experiments on finite open arrays reveal signatures consistent with these regimes, with response maps agreeing qualitatively with the calculated phase diagram.
AI.conclusion: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays are established as tools for exploring frustrated, material-motivated Hamiltonians, motivating searches for new quantum-driven magnetization plateaus and quantum-dimer behavior in ErB4 under a transverse field or in strain-tuned TmB4.

title: Trainable Quantum-Native Language Models: Dissipative Memory, Capacity Limits, and Hardware Validation
summary: We study byte-level autoregressive language models whose hidden state is a small quantum register, whose transitions are learned token-conditioned quantum channels, and whose next-byte probabilities come directly from Born-rule measurements without a learned classical vocabulary projection or softmax. In the fixed-width recurrent setting, unitary dynamics cannot contract or reset stored distinctions; experimentally, unitary recurrence loses to its retrained one-token control in every tested variant. Introducing learned dissipation, then token-conditioned dissipative gating, yields useful memory beyond one token. The gated model improves test negative log-likelihood by 0.20 +/- 0.03 nats/byte over retrained parameter-matched one-token controls at context length 12, and by 0.29-0.33 at longer contexts, but never beats retrained two-token controls. A key-value recall benchmark shows a width-dependent threshold: one stored pair meets the pre-registered accuracy bar at 4-5 memory qubits, two pairs at 6-7, and three pairs remain unsolved. This is consistent with, but does not establish, a capacity explanation for the short effective memory horizon. As a secondary result, one-qubit models reach lower stationary memory entropy than a heuristically optimized classical predictive frontier at matched error in 9/9 seeds. On IBM Heron hardware, computational-basis memory-register distributions show signal against a uniform null in 12/12 circuits across prefixes of up to 12 tokens, next-bit probabilities pass pre-registered accuracy bars at four-token prefixes, and bytes are generated autoregressively by sampling physically measured bit probabilities. The tested models are classically simulable and substantially worse than classical n-gram baselines. We claim no computational quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper studies byte-level autoregressive language models built on a small quantum register with learned token-conditioned quantum channels and Born-rule readout (no classical softmax). Unitary recurrence fails; learned dissipation/gating enables memory beyond one token but never beats a retrained two-token control, with narrow recall capacity and no claimed quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to explore whether a small quantum register can serve as the hidden state of a byte-level autoregressive language model, replacing a classical vocabulary projection/softmax with Born-rule measurements, and to test whether quantum recurrence and dissipation can provide useful memory beyond trivial one-token contexts.
AI.method: They train byte-level autoregressive models whose hidden state is a small quantum register, with transitions as learned token-conditioned quantum channels and next-byte probabilities from Born-rule measurements. They compare fixed-width recurrent variants against retrained parameter-matched one-token and two-token controls, introduce learned dissipation and token-conditioned dissipative gating, evaluate a key-value recall benchmark by memory-qubit width, run one-qubit stationary memory-entropy comparisons against a classical predictive frontier, and execute memory-register measurements on IBM Heron hardware for up to 12-token prefixes.
AI.result: Unitary recurrence loses to its retrained one-token control in every tested variant. With learned dissipation and token-conditioned dissipative gating, the model improves test NLL by 0.20 +/- 0.03 nats/byte over one-token controls at context length 12 and by 0.29-0.33 at longer contexts, but never beats retrained two-token controls. Recall shows a width-dependent threshold: one stored pair at 4-5 memory qubits, two pairs at 6-7, three pairs unsolved. One-qubit models reach lower stationary memory entropy than a heuristic classical predictive frontier at matched error in 9/9 seeds. On IBM Heron hardware, memory-register distributions show signal against a uniform null in 12/12 circuits, and next-bit probabilities pass pre-registered accuracy bars at four-token prefixes.
AI.conclusion: Learned dissipation and token-conditioned dissipative gating give limited memory beyond one token, but the models remain classically simulable and substantially worse than classical n-gram baselines, with no claimed computational quantum advantage. The observed narrow effective memory horizon is consistent with, but does not establish, a capacity explanation.

title: Improved classical optimization of fermionic Hamiltonians beyond Gaussian states
summary: We give a polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm that approximates the largest eigenvalue $λ_{\max}$ of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian $H$ on $n$ modes. The algorithm achieves energy at least $λ_{\max}/O(\sqrt n)$ and outputs either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis. This is achieved through a new upper bound on $λ_{\max}$ in terms of the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and $\sqrt{2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(H^2)}$.

AI.tldr: A polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm approximates the largest eigenvalue of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian, achieving energy at least λ_max/O(√n) and outputting a fermionic Gaussian or polynomially sparse Fock-basis state, enabled by a new upper bound on λ_max.
AI.motivation: Estimating the largest eigenvalue (ground-state energy) of quartic fermionic Hamiltonians is a fundamental and generally hard problem; the paper seeks an efficient classical approximation with provable guarantees.
AI.method: A polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm, grounded in a new upper bound on λ_max expressed via the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and the quantity √(2^{-n} Tr(H²)).
AI.result: The algorithm attains energy at least λ_max/O(√n) and returns either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis.
AI.conclusion: Traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonians admit an efficient classical approximation to their largest eigenvalue within a 1/O(√n) factor, with the new eigenvalue upper bound as the key technical ingredient.

title: Classification of bipartite observables II: NIP observables and the Todorcevic trichotomy
summary: A bipartite observable is stable when its idealized responses are continuous. We show that it is NIP exactly when they are of the first Baire class. They then form a Rosenthal compactum, and the dividing lines of Shelah in model theory, together with the classification of Rosenthal compacta of Todorčević, acquire a physical meaning. For observables, mixtures of states make every hereditarily separable compactum of idealized responses metrizable, and the Todorčević trichotomy becomes a classification into three classes. Each class contains a physical order: the comparison of photon numbers, the comparison of positions, and the causal order of spacetime, whose idealized responses are not first countable because a light cone can shrink to a point; the comparison of two phases on a circle joins it there. Each of the seven minimal families of the heptachotomy, which Argyros, Dodos and Kanellopoulos extracted from the methods of Todorčević, is realized by a tree of preparations of photons, of a particle in a box, or of a spin chain read by a probe; the spin chain also shows that NIP, unlike its uniform version, is not symmetric between the two parties. Finally, for the Ising model in a transverse field we show that, in the ordered phase, the responses of the two pure phases form split pairs whose midpoints, the responses of the symmetric state, form an uncountable discrete set; the proof uses a Lee--Yang theorem for this model.

AI.tldr: Bipartite observables with stable (continuous) idealized responses are NIP iff their responses are of the first Baire class, yielding a Rosenthal compactum and giving physical meaning to Shelah's dividing lines and Todorčević's classification; three physical orders (photon number, position, causal) exemplify the trichotomy, seven minimal heptachotomy families are realized physically, NIP is shown non-symmetric, and the transverse-field Ising model's ordered phase yields split pairs with uncountable discrete midpoint set.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to connect model-theoretic dividing lines (Shelah's NIP) and topological classification of Rosenthal compacta (Todorčević) to concrete physical observables, giving these abstract classifications physical meaning and providing physical realizations of the heptachotomy's minimal families.
AI.method: It characterizes stable bipartite observables via Baire class one responses and Rosenthal compacta; analyzes three physical orders (photon number comparison, position comparison, causal order) under the Todorčević trichotomy; realizes each of the seven minimal heptachotomy families via trees of preparations of photons, a particle in a box, or a spin chain read by a probe; and studies the transverse-field Ising model, using a Lee–Yang theorem to analyze split pairs and midpoint responses in the ordered phase.
AI.result: NIP holds exactly when idealized responses are of the first Baire class, forming a Rosenthal compactum; mixtures of states make every hereditarily separable compactum of responses metrizable; the trichotomy classifies into three classes each containing a physical order, with the causal order failing first countability due to light cones shrinking to a point; all seven minimal heptachotomy families are physically realized; NIP is not symmetric between parties (spin chain); the Ising ordered phase yields split pairs whose midpoint responses (symmetric state) form an uncountable discrete set.
AI.conclusion: Abstract model-theoretic and topological classifications of observable responses acquire concrete physical meaning, with physical systems (photons, particle in a box, spin chains, Ising model) realizing the dividing lines and heptachotomy families, and revealing features such as non-symmetry of NIP and uncountable discrete response sets in ordered phases.

title: An Instability of the Quantum Markov Length
summary: The Markov length, the length scale governing the exponential decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) in a quantum many-body state, has proven useful for characterizing mixed-state phases of matter. Nevertheless, we show that a state's Markov length is not generally stable under weak local channels. The failure of stability occurs already at a pure product state. We demonstrate this explicitly in a one-dimensional fermionic chain, where a fine-tuned depth-two circuit of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels maps the vacuum to a state whose CMI decays \emph{algebraically} and whose Markov length is therefore infinite, even when the channels are taken arbitrarily close to the identity. The algebraic decay is rooted in the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators. We exhibit an analogous instability on an ordinary qubit chain. More generally, we show that the Markov length is unstable in any translation-invariant state with even a single rank-deficient reduced density operator. These results pose a challenge to recent definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence based on the Markov length.

AI.tldr: The Markov length (governing exponential decay of conditional mutual information) is generally unstable under weak local channels: a fine-tuned depth-two Gaussian circuit maps a pure product state to one with algebraically decaying CMI and infinite Markov length, challenging Markov-length-based definitions of mixed-state phases.
AI.motivation: The Markov length has proven useful for characterizing mixed-state phases of matter, and recent definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence rely on it. The authors test whether this quantity is stable under weak local channels—a prerequisite for it to serve as a robust phase diagnostic—and find it is not.
AI.method: Construct a one-dimensional fermionic chain and apply a fine-tuned depth-two circuit of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels to the vacuum, taking the channels arbitrarily close to the identity. Analyze the resulting conditional mutual information (CMI) decay and link it to the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators. Reproduce the instability on an ordinary qubit chain, and generalize to any translation-invariant state with at least one rank-deficient reduced density operator.
AI.result: The state produced from a pure product state exhibits CMI decaying algebraically rather than exponentially, yielding an infinite Markov length even for channels near the identity. The instability occurs already at a pure product state, and is shown analytically on a qubit chain and for any translation-invariant state with a single rank-deficient reduced density operator.
AI.conclusion: Markov length is not stable under weak local channels, so definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence based on it are challenged and require reconsideration.

title: Quantum-assisted rendezvous on hypercubes: a quantum Bernoulli noise approach
summary: We study quantum-assisted balanced rendezvous on the $d$-dimensional hypercube in a one-step two-agent quantum-walk framework, where the two agents move the same Hamming distance and meet at a common midpoint. The key structure is a projective $t$-sphere resolution, which governs exact finite-dimensional quantum attainment. Its scalar analogue recovers the corresponding classical characterization. We characterize finite-dimensional quantum attainment of the no-signalling benchmark, construct quantum strategies from projective sphere resolutions, and establish a rigidity theorem for optimal finite-dimensional strategies. A marked difference appears between nearest-neighbor and higher-cardinality updates: quantum advantage can occur in the former, whereas in the latter the geometry of the relevant Hamming spheres rules out exact finite-dimensional attainment of the no-signalling value. Together, these results connect quantum-walk dynamics, Hamming-sphere geometry, and quantum rendezvous within the quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN) framework.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum-assisted balanced rendezvous of two agents on the d-dimensional hypercube using a one-step two-agent quantum-walk framework, where agents move equal Hamming distance and meet at a midpoint. By introducing projective t-sphere resolutions, the authors characterize finite-dimensional quantum attainment of the no-signalling benchmark, construct quantum strategies, prove a rigidity theorem for optimal finite-dimensional strategies, and distinguish nearest-neighbor from higher-cardinality updates regarding quantum advantage, all within the quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN) framework.
AI.motivation: Balanced rendezvous on hypercube graphs is a natural meeting-point problem in which two agents must coordinate despite moving symmetrically. Connecting such coordination tasks to quantum-walk dynamics, Hamming-sphere geometry, and no-signalling benchmarks motivates understanding when finite-dimensional quantum strategies can exactly attain no-signalling values, and how locality (nearest-neighbor vs. higher-cardinality moves) affects quantum advantage. The paper aims to clarify these attainability limits and structural properties.
AI.method: The authors analyze a one-step two-agent quantum walk on the d-dimensional hypercube where both agents move the same Hamming distance to a common midpoint. They introduce a projective t-sphere resolution as the core algebraic/geometric structure controlling exact finite-dimensional quantum attainment, with its scalar analogue recovering the classical characterization. Using this structure they characterize finite-dimensional quantum attainment of the no-signalling benchmark, explicitly construct quantum strategies from projective sphere resolutions, and prove a rigidity theorem for optimal finite-dimensional strategies. The analysis is set within the quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN) framework.
AI.result: The paper characterizes finite-dimensional quantum attainment of the no-signalling benchmark and provides constructive quantum strategies derived from projective sphere resolutions, along with a rigidity theorem for optimal finite-dimensional strategies. A marked distinction is established: for nearest-neighbor updates quantum advantage can occur, whereas for higher-cardinality updates the geometry of the relevant Hamming spheres rules out exact finite-dimensional attainment of the no-signalling value.
AI.conclusion: Projective t-sphere resolutions govern exact finite-dimensional quantum attainment in balanced hypercube rendezvous, unifying quantum-walk dynamics, Hamming-sphere geometry, and quantum rendezvous within the QBN framework. The results reveal that quantum advantage depends critically on move cardinality, with nearest-neighbor updates permitting advantage while higher-cardinality updates preclude exact finite-dimensional attainment of the no-signalling value.

title: Quantum Information-Theoretic Analysis of Optical Fiber Sensing via Stimulated Brillouin Scattering
summary: Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) is a powerful mechanism for distributed sensing in optical fibers, as the Brillouin response is highly sensitive to local material parameters. Assuming the input probe is a quantum state, we develop a quantum-information-theoretic framework for SBS-based fiber sensing and intrusion detection. Starting from a linearized opto-acoustic Hamiltonian, we derive an effective input-output relation for a short fiber segment. We then model each fiber segment as a single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel and the entire fiber as a cascade of quantum channels. We then compute the quantum Fisher information for general SBS-dependent parameters and identify optimal measurement settings to achieve the quantum limit, comparing them with receiver-constrained strategies such as heterodyne detection and photon counting. In addition, we propose an adaptive approach that achieves first-order asymptotic optimality and provides a novel second-order correction to address preliminary miscalibration. As an application, we apply the framework to the fiber-tapping detection problem.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a quantum-information-theoretic framework for SBS-based fiber sensing and intrusion detection, modeling fiber segments as bosonic Gaussian channels, deriving quantum Fisher information, identifying optimal measurements, and proposing an adaptive strategy.
AI.motivation: SBS is a powerful mechanism for distributed sensing because the Brillouin response is highly sensitive to local material parameters. However, a quantum treatment of the input probe state and its implications for sensing limits and optimal detection strategies had not been systematically addressed.
AI.method: Starting from a linearized opto-acoustic Hamiltonian, the authors derive an effective input-output relation for a short fiber segment, model each segment as a single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel, and represent the whole fiber as a cascade of quantum channels. They compute the quantum Fisher information for general SBS-dependent parameters and identify optimal measurement settings, comparing them with receiver-constrained strategies. They also propose an adaptive approach for asymptotic optimality with a second-order correction.
AI.result: Optimal measurement settings are identified that achieve the quantum limit and are benchmarked against heterodyne detection and photon counting. The proposed adaptive approach attains first-order asymptotic optimality and provides a novel second-order correction for preliminary miscalibration. The framework is applied to fiber-tapping detection.
AI.conclusion: A quantum-information-theoretic treatment of SBS-based fiber sensing yields fundamental limits and practical measurement strategies, with the adaptive method offering near-optimal performance and robustness to miscalibration, demonstrated on the fiber-tapping detection problem.

title: When irrelevance governs: dissipation-regression scaling in open quantum criticality
comment: 10 pages, no figure. Substantially extended from 2607.11206v1
summary: The real-time dynamics of quantum phase transitions in open systems coupled to finite-temperature environments sits at the heart of contemporary condensed-matter and quantum-information science. Here, invoking a Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, we uncover that, within the coherence-dominated regime of critical real-time evolution, a dissipative coupling deemed naively irrelevant determines, counterintuitively, the longest timescale that holds sway. Possessing a well-defined temporal scaling dimension, it engenders a novel dissipation-regression scaling that systematically reproduces the unusual Kibble-Zurek scaling and relaxation observed in recent numerical studies. By contrast, dissipation-dominated dynamics behaves qualitatively differently. There, furthermore, we show that the discretized and diagonalized formulations of the same open quantum Ising chain realize distinct universality classes.

AI.tldr: Using a Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, the authors show that a naively irrelevant dissipative coupling governs the longest timescale in coherence-dominated critical real-time evolution of open quantum systems, yielding a novel dissipation-regression scaling that reproduces anomalous Kibble-Zurek behavior. Dissipation-dominated dynamics instead behaves qualitatively differently, and discretized versus diagonalized formulations of the same open quantum Ising chain belong to distinct universality classes.
AI.motivation: Real-time dynamics of quantum phase transitions in open systems coupled to finite-temperature environments is central to condensed-matter and quantum-information science, but the scaling behavior of such critical real-time evolution—especially anomalous Kibble-Zurek scaling seen in numerics—lacks a clear theoretical account.
AI.method: The authors invoke a Schwinger-Keldysh formalism to analyze critical real-time evolution of an open quantum Ising chain, characterizing dissipative couplings through their temporal scaling dimension, and compare coherence-dominated versus dissipation-dominated regimes as well as discretized and diagonalized formulations.
AI.result: In the coherence-dominated regime, a dissipative coupling naively deemed irrelevant actually sets the longest timescale; it possesses a well-defined temporal scaling dimension and generates a novel dissipation-regression scaling that systematically reproduces the unusual Kibble-Zurek scaling and relaxation seen in recent numerical studies. Dissipation-dominated dynamics is qualitatively different, and the discretized and diagonalized formulations of the same open quantum Ising chain realize distinct universality classes.
AI.conclusion: Irrelevant-looking dissipation can control the slowest critical timescales via a dissipation-regression scaling, the two dissipation regimes are qualitatively distinct, and the choice of formulation (discretized vs. diagonalized) can change the universality class of the same open quantum Ising chain.

title: Quantum-Circuit Residuals for Receptor Functional Potency Prediction: Predictive Gains and Quadratic Structure
comment: 37 pages,including 19 pages of Supporting Information; 5 figures
summary: The predictive performance of neural networks for receptor functional potency modeling depends on both molecular representations and prediction-head design. Using GLP-1R cAMP-related pEC50 prediction as the primary task, we jointly train a classical molecular encoder with a linear base head and a shallow quantum-circuit residual head that share the learned molecular representation. We evaluate the models using random and structure-group splits, include tuned Chemprop as a domain reference, and extend the evaluation to ADRB2 and MC4R. Under the GLP-1R structure-group split, the quantum-residual models reduce mean absolute error relative to the corresponding base models from 0.677 to 0.639 with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) encoder and from 0.680 to 0.641 with a graph neural network (GNN) encoder. In structural control experiments, a parameter-count-matched real-orthogonal control achieves similar predictive performance, suggesting that some quantum-residual gains may be associated with structured quadratic feature interactions. By combining receptor functional potency prediction with structural analysis of the quantum residual, this study provides empirical evidence to inform compact residual-head design and highlights the potential of quantum-circuit parameterizations for this task.

AI.tldr: A classical molecular encoder is jointly trained with a linear base head and a shallow quantum-circuit residual head, reducing MAE for receptor functional potency (pEC50) prediction, with gains partly attributable to structured quadratic feature interactions.

AI.method: Using GLP-1R cAMP-related pEC50 prediction as the primary task, a classical molecular encoder (MLP or GNN) is jointly trained with a linear base head and a shallow quantum-circuit residual head sharing the learned representation. Evaluation uses random and structure-group splits, includes tuned Chemprop as a domain reference, and extends to ADRB2 and MC4R, plus parameter-count-matched real-orthogonal control experiments.
AI.result: Under the GLP-1R structure-group split, quantum-residual models reduce MAE from 0.677 to 0.639 (MLP encoder) and from 0.680 to 0.641 (GNN encoder). The parameter-count-matched real-orthogonal control achieves similar predictive performance, suggesting some quantum-residual gains may stem from structured quadratic feature interactions.
AI.conclusion: Combining receptor functional potency prediction with structural analysis of the quantum residual, the study provides empirical evidence to inform compact residual-head design and highlights the potential of quantum-circuit parameterizations for this task.

title: Error Mitigation by Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) in Indirect-Control System
comment: 28 pages, 21 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in IEEE Access
summary: The indirect-control paradigm offers a scalable approach to quantum computation by restricting external operations to a small subset of qubits, whereas the entire system evolves under its intrinsic many-body Hamiltonian. This framework reduces hardware complexity and limits the noise introduced through control channels. Recently, Anan et al. proposed an implementation of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) within this indirect-control architecture. However, the impact and integration of quantum error mitigation techniques in such a setting remain largely unexplored. In particular, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), a widely used error mitigation strategy, has not yet been systematically adapted to indirect-control VQE. A key requirement of ZNE is the controlled amplification of noise, which is commonly achieved through circuit-level techniques such as unitary folding. In the indirect-control framework, however, quantum operations are largely governed by continuous time-evolution under the system Hamiltonian, making the construction of physically realizable inverse operations non-trivial. title: All-optical deconvolution via quantum cross-correlation spectroscopy with bright twin beams
summary: The resolution of spectroscopic measurements is fundamentally limited by the convolution between a system's intrinsic response and the instrument response function, creating an ill-posed inverse problem. While entangled photons can theoretically bypass these limits, low photon flux has hindered their experimental realization. Here, we propose quantum cross-correlation spectroscopy (QCCS), utilizing macroscopic twin beams (signal and idler beams) to physically circumvent this convolution limit in coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering. Employing the signal beam as a broadband probe, QCCS achieves all-optical deconvolution through a correlation-enhanced sum-frequency generation channel between the convoluted anti-Stokes and idler beams. By subtracting the uncorrelated background using a 500-femtosecond temporal window, we successfully retrieve narrow Raman bands (8 cm^{-1} and 15 cm^{-1}) completely obscured by a 75 cm^{-1} probe bandwidth without numerical deconvolution or prior knowledge. Our results establish macroscopic quantum correlations as a robust resource for high-fidelity spectroscopy, paving the way for ultrashort-pulse-free operando studies under natural, incoherent excitation conditions.

Although entangled photons could theoretically bypass this limit, their low photon flux has prevented experimental realization.
