title: A robust digital receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution utilizes advanced digital signal processing techniques to mitigate channel impairments, driving the progress of high-performance quantum secure communications. Specifically, digital heterodyne receivers are commonly implemented using down-conversion algorithms to detect both components simultaneously where the signal is modulated onto an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and bypass stringent optical phase-locking requirements. However, a rigorous analysis of the quantum security implications of the digital down-conversion algorithm remains absent. In this paper, we investigate the algorithm process from the perspective of quantum operator evolution, revealing that the frequency folding effect inherent in down-conversion inevitably mixes the image-frequency information into the baseband signal. To address this issue, we propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme based on dual-path digital heterodyne receiver. By performing a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain, this scheme perfectly cancels out the image-frequency operator physically. The robust receiver architecture preserves the baseband noise-suppression advantages, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric optical detection losses, and fundamentally closes the image-frequency crosstalk. Practical experiments have validated the feasibility of the proposed architecture and its effective suppression of image-frequency noise, achieving a performance of 11.4 Mbps @ 42 km. This work lays a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for future high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

AI.motivation: Digital heterodyne receivers in CV-QKD commonly use down-conversion to an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and relax optical phase-locking requirements, but a rigorous quantum-security analysis of this down-conversion algorithm has been missing. The inherent frequency-folding effect can compromise security by leaking image-frequency information into the baseband.

They then propose an operator reconstruction detection scheme based on a dual-path digital heterodyne receiver, applying a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators from two optical paths in the digital domain to cancel the image-frequency operator.
AI.result: The proposed architecture retains baseband noise-suppression benefits, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing under asymmetric optical detection losses, and closes image-frequency crosstalk. Experiments confirm feasibility and effective image-frequency noise suppression, achieving 11.4 Mbps at 42 km.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a theoretical and algorithmic foundation for high-performance, highly secure digital CV-QKD systems by resolving the security gap in down-conversion-based digital heterodyne detection.

title: Temporal-Access Resource Theory for Continuous Process Tensors
summary: The uncontrolled endpoint channel can conceal how well a quantum process can protect a logical task under time-resolved control. We formulate a fixed-task resource theory of continuous process tensors with physical access interfaces, entrance-erasing free objects, and budgeted free conversions. Complete-record total-variation error measures performance; the calibrated capability is monotone under conversions that preserve a common free baseline. For unknown-state transmission the baseline is exactly $1-d^{-2}$. Two qubit processes with the same endpoint channel have optimal errors $0$ and $p=\sin^2(2gh)$ at the same finite pulse budget in an ideal-transparent system-only window architecture, forcing any endpoint-only predictor to err by at least $p/2$ on one of them. An exactly solvable family shows how the allocation of a fixed interaction phase around a control window sets the attainable error, and a nontrivial perfect echo requires and attains total control action $π$ in that architecture. The separation extends directly to every qubit unitary target at a budget that includes its boundary gate, while unitary tasks in any dimension have baseline $1-d^{-2}$ whenever a budget-feasible free realization gives the depolarizing output. Complete-record implementation bounds quantify coherent and dissipative control imperfections. Continuous-process randomized compilation supplies physical instrument pullbacks; compatible completion conditions extend their action, and certified dynamical bounds yield achievable task-error and capability guarantees. The resulting theory identifies temporal structure and control investment that endpoint characterization alone cannot resolve.

AI.motivation: Endpoint (input-output) channel characterization is insufficient to capture how well a quantum process can protect a logical task under time-resolved control; two processes sharing the same endpoint channel can differ dramatically in achievable error depending on their internal temporal structure and control budget.

Use complete-record total-variation error as the performance measure and define a calibrated capability monotone under conversions preserving a common free baseline. Apply continuous-process randomized compilation to obtain physical instrument pullbacks, extend their action via compatible completion conditions, and derive certified dynamical bounds yielding task-error and capability guarantees.

title: Pulsed control of an entanglement-breaking index: thermal valleys, a certified valve, and its open-close asymmetry
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Ancillary files: certified channel model, search and certification pipeline, schedule engine, complete valley lists, certificate files and check scripts. Supersedes the valley, pulse and tilt analysis of arXiv:2609.09350v1-v2; companion to arXiv:2609.27908
summary: The entanglement-breaking index of a channel is the number of self-compositions after which all entanglement with a reference system is destroyed. In a thermal qubit collision loop whose round is affine in the bath polarisation p, some circuits have thermal valleys: on an interior window of p the index falls below its infinite-temperature value. Rounds at different p compose exactly, so every schedule of polarisations defines a composite channel whose entanglement-breaking status can be certified in ball arithmetic. A gated search of 33 million random circuits finds no valley with contrast above about 3e-3, with an interior maximum near index 90, and yields six certified targets. At the reference target, held inside its window for 88 rounds, a centred excursion to p = 0.05 restores entanglement at exactly eight rounds: every shorter centred pulse certifiably fails, and so do the same eight rounds at the start. A 53-round pulse certifiably beats the static protocol, a depth-three valley is walked down its staircase by pulse duration, and a 1.2 per cent coherent tilt of the ancilla opens the switch at fixed population. Closing the switch costs 21 to 35 rounds. The asymmetry is not one of local rates, which agree to within about two per cent at matched circuit positions (certified). It is one of distance and response: closing must remove an entanglement margin 2.2 times larger, and while hot rounds added to a window hold act almost independently, window rounds added to a hot hold act collectively. Near the crossing, the lever of the log-margin is that of a linear approach to the entanglement-breaking boundary, with no free parameter. At the reference target, depolarising noise of about $4ν/n$ per round kills a signature of size $ν$ read after $n$ rounds: 1.3e-4 for the static signal, 6.5e-6 for the eight-round switch.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the entanglement-breaking index (EBI) of thermal qubit collision loops whose round is affine in bath polarisation p, revealing interior "thermal valleys" where the EBI drops below its infinite-temperature value, and characterising gated, certified switching behaviour in such channels.
AI.motivation: Entanglement-breaking (EB) is the fundamental boundary separating channels that can transmit entanglement from those that cannot. Thermal collision loops, where each round composes with the bath polarisation, provide a controllable setting in which the EBI—the number of self-compositions needed to destroy entanglement—can exhibit non-monotonic behaviour such as interior "thermal valleys." Understanding, certifying, and exploiting such structure (especially protocols that switch EB status on and off) is the goal of this work.
AI.method: Rounds at different polarisations compose exactly, so any schedule of polarisations defines a composite channel whose EB status is certified using ball (interval) arithmetic. A gated search of 33 million random circuits probes for valleys, using certified targets where a centred excursion in p is tested at varying pulse durations and positions, alongside comparisons to static protocols, depth-three staircase valleys, ancilla tilt, and local-rate matching.
AI.result: The search finds no valley with contrast above about 3e-3, with an interior maximum near index 90, yielding six certified targets. At the reference target (held in-window for 88 rounds), a centred excursion to p = 0.05 restores entanglement at exactly eight rounds: every shorter centred pulse certifiably fails, as do the same eight rounds at the start. A 53-round pulse certifiably beats the static protocol, a depth-three valley is walked down its staircase by pulse duration, and a 1.2% coherent tilt of the ancilla opens the switch at fixed population. Closing the switch costs 21 to 35 rounds. Local rates agree to within about 2% at matched circuit positions (certified); the asymmetry resides in distance and response instead—closing must remove an entanglement margin 2.2 times larger, and hot rounds added to a window hold act almost independently while window rounds added to a hot hold act collectively. Near the crossing, the lever of the log-margin matches a linear approach to the EB boundary with no free parameter. Depolarising noise of about 4ν/n per round kills a signature of size ν read after n rounds: 1.3e-4 for the static signal and 6.5e-6 for the eight-round switch.
AI.conclusion: Thermal collision loops exhibit interior thermal valleys and sharp, certifiable entanglement-breaking switching behaviour. The switch is highly asymmetric: opening is achieved by a precise eight-round pulse while closing requires 21–35 rounds, an asymmetry driven not by differing local rates but by distance to the EB boundary and collective versus independent response. The log-margin lever follows a no-free-parameter linear approach to the EB boundary, and depolarising noise imposes a strict per-round budget that the eight-round switch tolerates far better than the static protocol.

title: Continuous-wave AC magnetometry up to hundreds of megahertz using nitrogen-vacancy centers under a strong transverse magnetic field
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, submit to Applied Physics Letters
summary: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are promising quantum sensors for AC magnetic fields. However, conventional dynamical-decoupling-based magnetometry becomes technically demanding at high frequencies because of the requirement for increasingly short and high-power microwave pulses. This paper describes an AC magnetometry technique based on continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR) measurements, which enables the detection of signals in the hundred-MHz range. By applying a strong static magnetic field transverse to the NV axis, the energy separation between the relevant electron-spin states was tuned and resonantly coupled with the target radiofrequency (RF) magnetic field, thereby forming RF-dressed states. Unlike pulsed dynamical-decoupling schemes, this approach does not require high-power microwave pulse sequences. The key feature of our method is that the detectable frequency can be tuned by controlling the bias magnetic field strength. Using this methodology, we have experimentally achieved the frequency-tunable detection of AC magnetic fields from 14.4-632 MHz. The sensitivity was 0.558 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 14.4 MHz and 24.4 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 632 MHz. We characterized the field-dependent ODMR contrast and linewidth, and found that their degradation at large transverse fields is a important factor limiting the high-frequency sensitivity. These results establish a simple CW-ODMR approach for widely tunable RF magnetic-field sensing without high-power pulsed spin control.

AI.tldr: A CW-ODMR-based AC magnetometry technique uses transverse bias fields to form RF-dressed NV spin states, enabling tunable detection of AC magnetic fields from 14.4 to 632 MHz without high-power pulsed spin control.
AI.motivation: Conventional dynamical-decoupling magnetometry with NV centers requires increasingly short and high-power microwave pulses at high frequencies, making it technically demanding. There is a need for a simpler approach that can detect high-frequency AC magnetic fields without pulsed spin control.
AI.method: Apply a strong static magnetic field transverse to the NV axis to tune the energy separation between relevant electron-spin states and resonantly couple them with the target RF magnetic field, forming RF-dressed states. Detection is performed via continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR), with the detectable frequency tuned by controlling the bias magnetic field strength.
AI.result: Experimentally achieved frequency-tunable AC magnetic field detection from 14.4 to 632 MHz, with sensitivities of 0.558 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 14.4 MHz and 24.4 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 632 MHz. Field-dependent ODMR contrast and linewidth were characterized, showing that their degradation at large transverse fields limits high-frequency sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a simple CW-ODMR approach for widely tunable RF magnetic-field sensing without high-power pulsed spin control, offering a practical alternative to dynamical-decoupling schemes at high frequencies.

title: Verifiable Sampling for Delegated Generative Quantum Machine Learning
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI 2026). \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE
summary:
Generative machine learning has shown remarkable results across a wide range of interdisciplinary tasks, motivating significant efforts toward Quantum Generative Models as a path to beyond-classical performance, given their capability of generating classically intractable distributions. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to securely delegating such computations to a powerful remote quantum server. In this work, we propose a blind and verifiable protocol for sampling that can be used for the inference phase of such quantum models. Such a protocol inherits blindness from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and achieves verifiability by exploiting known approaches based on trapification schemes. Alongside, to delegate the training phase, we discuss an extension of the previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms (Inajetovic et al., Phys. Rev. Research, 2026).
  Beyond the usual Accept/Abort outcome characterizing verification protocols, the sampling protocol for inference also provides, even against a malicious server, an estimation of the amount of corrupted generated samples, i.e., a fine-grained feature describing the quality of the outcome connecting verification protocols and application-level benchmarking.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a blind and verifiable protocol for delegating the sampling (inference) phase of Quantum Generative Models to an untrusted remote quantum server, built on Universal Blind Quantum Computing for blindness and trapification for verifiability, and uniquely providing a fine-grained estimate of the number of corrupted generated samples rather than just an Accept/Abort verdict.
AI.motivation: Quantum Generative Models promise beyond-classical performance by generating classically intractable distributions, yet little attention has been given to securely delegating these computations to a powerful but potentially untrusted remote quantum server. There is a need for protocols ensuring both privacy (blindness) of the client's computation and correctness (verifiability) of the server's output during inference and training.
AI.method: The authors design a blind and verifiable sampling protocol for the inference phase of quantum generative models. Blindness is inherited from Universal Blind Quantum Computing (UBQC), while verifiability is achieved via trapification-based schemes. For the training phase, they extend a previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithm (Inajetovic et al., Phys. Rev. Research, 2026). The protocol additionally outputs an estimate of the number of corrupted generated samples, going beyond the standard Accept/Abort verification outcome.
AI.result: The protocol securely delegates sampling-based inference while preserving blindness and offering verifiability. Even against a malicious server, it provides a fine-grained estimate of the amount of corrupted generated samples, thereby characterizing output quality. A verifiable end-to-end delegation approach is also discussed for the training phase via extension of prior Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The work connects verification protocols with application-level benchmarking by delivering a quantitative quality measure of the generated samples instead of a binary Accept/Abort decision. This advances secure delegation of both inference and training for Quantum Generative Models on remote quantum servers.

title: Block encoding of semiseparable matrices via their generators
summary: We present an explicit quantum circuit that constructs a block encoding of a generator-representable semiseparable (one-pair) matrix directly from its two generators. For an $N\times N$ semiseparable matrix with $N=2^{n}$, the circuit uses $2n+2$ ancilla qubits and has $O({\rm polylog} N)$ depth, and it realizes a $(2\sqrt{N},\,2n+2,\,2 \sqrt{2}\ \varepsilon)$-block encoding, where $\varepsilon$ is controlled by the accuracy of the state-preparation routines that load the generators. The building blocks of the circuit are cyclic shifts, swaps, and Hadamard gates, each admitting an efficient implementation through the binary decomposition of the relevant indices.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an explicit quantum circuit that block-encodes a generator-representable semiseparable (one-pair) matrix directly from its two generators, using only 2n+2 ancilla qubits and O(polylog N) depth.
AI.motivation: Block encodings underpin many quantum algorithms (e.g., matrix arithmetic, QSVT), but constructing them for structured large matrices usually requires oracle access or costly decompositions. Semiseparable matrices are highly structured and appear in integral equations and control theory, so a direct, resource-efficient block-encoding from their compact generators is desirable.
AI.method: Exploit the one-pair semiseparable structure, where the matrix is fully determined by two generator vectors/scalars. Construct an explicit circuit built entirely from cyclic shifts, swaps, and Hadamard gates, implemented efficiently via binary decomposition of the relevant indices. State-preparation routines load the generators, and the ancilla register of 2n+2 qubits mediates the block encoding.
AI.result: For an N×N matrix with N=2^n, the circuit uses 2n+2 ancilla qubits and achieves O(polylog N) depth, realizing a (2√N, 2n+2, 2√2 ε)-block encoding, where ε is governed by the accuracy of the generator state-preparation routines.
AI.conclusion: Generator-representable semiseparable matrices admit explicit, low-depth quantum block encodings constructed directly from their generators, with polylogarithmic depth and a small ancilla overhead, enabling their use in quantum linear-algebra and related quantum algorithms.

title: Zak Phase Quantization without Global Symmetry through Destructive Interference
summary: The Zak phase provides a fundamental geometric characterization of one-dimensional band structures and, when quantized by symmetry, serves as a bulk indicator of polarization and boundary phenomena. Conventionally, its exact quantization is tied to a global symmetry of the Bloch Hamiltonian, such as inversion or reflection symmetry. Here, we demonstrate a distinct mechanism by which the Zak phase remains exactly quantized even when the corresponding protecting symmetry is explicitly broken at the level of the full Hamiltonian. The mechanism is based on local support symmetry and destructive interference: symmetry-breaking degrees of freedom are coupled to a topological parent system in such a way that the relevant Bloch states cannot leak into them. The preserved states therefore retain their parent wave functions and inherit their quantized Zak phase exactly, despite the absence of the protecting global symmetry. We establish this mechanism for general one-dimensional insulators and demonstrate it in an inversion-broken minimal model and a reflection-broken armchair nanoribbon, where a quantized $π$ Zak phase and associated boundary-localized states persist. We further show that perturbations violating the exact destructive-interference condition continuously dequantize the Zak phase, while a finite regime with a near-$π$ Zak phase and boundary response can survive. Our results establish wave-function support, rather than global symmetry alone, as a mechanism for protecting quantized quantum geometry in one-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: The Zak phase can remain exactly quantized even without a protecting global symmetry, via a mechanism based on local support symmetry and destructive interference, where symmetry-breaking degrees of freedom decouple from the relevant Bloch states.
AI.motivation: Conventionally, exact quantization of the Zak phase is attributed to a global symmetry (e.g., inversion or reflection) of the Bloch Hamiltonian. This work seeks a distinct mechanism that preserves exact quantization of the Zak phase even when the protecting global symmetry is explicitly broken.
AI.method: The authors introduce a mechanism relying on local support symmetry and destructive interference: symmetry-breaking degrees of freedom are coupled to a topological parent system such that the relevant Bloch states cannot leak into them, so the preserved states inherit the parent wave functions and their quantized Zak phase. They establish this for general 1D insulators and demonstrate it in two models: an inversion-broken minimal model and a reflection-broken armchair nanoribbon. They also analyze perturbations that violate the exact destructive-interference condition.
AI.result: In the inversion-broken minimal model and the reflection-broken armchair nanoribbon, a quantized π Zak phase and associated boundary-localized states persist despite broken global symmetry. Perturbations violating the exact destructive-interference condition continuously dequantize the Zak phase, while a finite regime with a near-π Zak phase and boundary response can survive.
AI.conclusion: Wave-function support, rather than global symmetry alone, acts as a mechanism protecting quantized quantum geometry in one-dimensional systems.

title: Circuit Design Problems in Binary Polynomial Quantum Optimization
summary: Solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum computers mainly relies on their quadratic unconstrained binary formulation. Lately, binary polynomial formulations start to take the center stage, having a better scaling with respect to the number of used qubits. However, while quadratic forms are straightforward to implement on quantum circuits, polynomial forms of degree $d$ incur in circuit depth overheads, due to the lack of $d$-qubit gates, for $d\geq 3$, on current hardware. In this paper, we study the problem of designing the shallowest quantum circuit for a given polynomial form. We formulate it as a classical binary linear problem and we prove the \textsf{NP}-completeness of a variant of it. On the algorithmic side, we offer a scalable and performant heuristic method to tackle it, Tempura, as well as faster binary linear problem formulations, which offer computational feasibility while sacrificing optimality. Our performance evaluation shows that the algorithms yield far shorter circuits than the state-of-the-art approaches, and Tempura is mostly comparable with them in terms of runtime.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of designing the shallowest quantum circuit for a given polynomial form used in combinatorial optimization. It formulates the problem as a classical binary linear problem, proves NP-completeness of a variant, and proposes a scalable heuristic (Tempura) plus faster relaxed formulations. Evaluation shows significantly shorter circuits than state-of-the-art methods, with Tempura's runtime largely comparable.
AI.motivation: Quadratic unconstrained binary formulations are standard for combinatorial optimization on near-term quantum computers, but binary polynomial formulations scale better in qubit count. Yet polynomial forms of degree d≥3 are costly in circuit depth because current hardware lacks d-qubit gates, so minimizing circuit depth for a given polynomial form is critical.
AI.method: The circuit-depth minimization problem for a given polynomial form is cast as a classical binary linear problem. The authors prove NP-completeness of a variant, and develop a scalable, performant heuristic called Tempura, along with faster binary linear problem formulations that trade optimality for computational feasibility.
AI.result: The proposed algorithms produce far shorter circuits than state-of-the-art approaches, and Tempura's runtime is mostly comparable to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Efficient circuit-depth optimization for high-degree polynomial forms is achievable via classical binary linear formulations and the Tempura heuristic, yielding substantially shallower circuits and competitive runtimes.

title: A General Method for Extending Isoscattering Non-Isospectral Quantum Graphs
summary: The present paper sets out a general method for extending the isoscattering, non-isospectral quantum graphs. The methodology is illustrated by considering two graphs, denoted by $Γ_1$ and $Γ_2$, which have the same total metric length but different topologies. It is demonstrated that, despite the fact that their scattering matrices are identical, their eigenvalues, denoted by $k_n$, and Euler characteristics differ from one another. The next step in the process is to extend both graphs by affixing the same star graph to each of them. Utilising the Titchmarsh-Weyl M-function formalism, it is proven that the newly constructed, extended graphs are also isoscattering and non-isospectral.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a general method to construct extended quantum graphs that remain isoscattering yet non-isospectral, demonstrated by attaching an identical star graph to two topologically distinct but equal-length graphs, and proving the extended pair preserves the same spectral properties via the Titchmarsh-Weyl M-function formalism.
AI.motivation: Isoscattering, non-isospectral quantum graphs (identical scattering matrices but different eigenvalues and Euler characteristics) are of interest, but a general method for extending them while preserving these properties was lacking.
AI.method: Two graphs Γ1 and Γ2 with equal total metric length but different topologies are considered. The same star graph is affixed to each, and the Titchmarsh-Weyl M-function formalism is used to analyze the resulting extended graphs.
AI.result: The two original graphs share identical scattering matrices, yet their eigenvalues k_n and Euler characteristics differ. After extension by the same star graph, the new extended graphs are shown to be both isoscattering and non-isospectral.
AI.conclusion: The proposed extension procedure is general and preserves the isoscattering, non-isospectral property, providing a systematic way to generate new such quantum graph pairs.

title: System-Design Optimization of a Single-Transmitter, Single-Fiber QKD-based ITS Communication Link
summary: Deploying QKD-based secure communication at scale requires reducing duplicated optical hardware while preserving the rate of protected user data. Earlier studies established the physical feasibility of carrying CV-QKD and classical signals over shared infrastructure, motivating a quantitative comparison between optical hardware savings and the OTP-encrypted rate. We perform this comparison by defining the secure communication rate (SCR) as the rate jointly supported by secret-key generation and classical transport, and using it to optimize a shared discrete-modulation CV-QKD link. The model combines a binomial 64-QAM security bound with a trusted receiver, protocol traffic, spectral leakage - optical power leaking into the quantum receive band - and Raman scattering. At 25 km, the asymptotic model gives an optimized SCR of 12.079 Mbps, compared with 12.095 Mbps for a separated-link reference, while reducing the transmitter and fiber counts from two to one each in the modeled direction. Increasing channel separation suppresses spectral leakage, but the resulting SCR gain diminishes once receiver bandwidth limits the rate. Under the adopted receiver-noise law, increasing the bandwidth budget from 350 to 750 MHz raises the projected 25-km SCR to 24.535 Mbps despite higher trusted electronic noise. For the studied metropolitan link, sharing saves optical resources with little rate loss, while receiver-bandwidth improvements provide greater benefit than further spectral separation. Together, these results suggest an integration path: share the transmitter and fiber, limit unwanted classical power in the quantum receive band, and increase usable receiver bandwidth where the noise budget permits.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies the trade-off between optical hardware savings and OTP-encrypted secure communication rate when CV-QKD and classical signals share transmitter and fiber, showing near-parity with separated links while bandwidth scaling yields larger gains.
AI.motivation: Scaling QKD-based secure communication requires reducing duplicated optical hardware without sacrificing the rate of protected user data. Prior work only established physical feasibility of co-propagating CV-QKD and classical signals over shared infrastructure, leaving a quantitative comparison between hardware savings and protected (OTP-encrypted) rate unexplored.
AI.method: Defines a secure communication rate (SCR) as the rate jointly supported by secret-key generation and classical transport, and uses it to optimize a shared discrete-modulation CV-QKD link. The model integrates a binomial 64-QAM security bound, a trusted receiver, protocol traffic, spectral leakage (classical optical power leaking into the quantum receive band), and Raman scattering. It compares the shared link against a separated-link reference and sweeps channel separation and receiver bandwidth.
AI.result: At 25 km, the asymptotic model yields an optimized SCR of 12.079 Mbps versus 12.095 Mbps for the separated-link reference, while halving transmitter and fiber counts (two to one each) in the modeled direction. Increasing channel separation suppresses spectral leakage, but the SCR gain saturates once receiver bandwidth limits the rate. Raising the bandwidth budget from 350 to 750 MHz lifts the projected 25-km SCR to 24.535 Mbps despite higher trusted electronic noise.
AI.conclusion: For the studied metropolitan link, resource sharing saves optical hardware with little rate loss, while receiver-bandwidth improvements deliver greater benefit than further spectral separation. The results suggest an integration path: share transmitter and fiber, limit unwanted classical power in the quantum receive band, and increase usable receiver bandwidth where the noise budget permits.

title: Wideband microwave resonator for NV center vector magnetometry
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color center in diamond has found applications in magnetometry across various geometrical scales. In particular, vector magnetometry using hand-held devices with low power consumption is of interest for mobile and geological applications. However, such a device requires efficient driving of the four different orientations of the NV center, thus placing demands on a broadband microwave resonator that provides a uniform and highly insensitive microwave magnetic field at the resonance frequencies of the NV centers. Here, we propose a unique planar resonator design that enables efficient driving of all four orientations of NV color centers over a 100 MHz range with only 0.5 W of microwave input power and 250 mW of laser power, allowing vector magnetic field measurements. Using the planar resonator to drive NV centers in diamond, a compact vector magnetometer was fabricated and experimentally studied. The sensitivity of the device is about \[{1.2\text{ nT}}/{\sqrt{\text{Hz}}}\;\]. While this is not a record sensitivity for diamond-based magnetometers, this device occupies its own niche as a compact hand-held magnetometer.

AI.tldr: A compact, hand-held vector magnetometer using a unique planar microwave resonator that efficiently drives all four NV center orientations over a 100 MHz range with low power (0.5 W microwave, 250 mW laser), achieving ~1.2 nT/√Hz sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Vector magnetometry with hand-held, low-power devices is desirable for mobile and geological applications. However, driving the four different NV center orientations requires a broadband microwave resonator that provides a uniform and highly orientation-insensitive microwave magnetic field at the NV resonance frequencies.
AI.method: The authors propose a unique planar resonator design enabling efficient driving of all four NV color center orientations over a 100 MHz range using only 0.5 W microwave input power and 250 mW laser power. This planar resonator drives NV centers in diamond to build a compact vector magnetometer, which was then experimentally studied.
AI.result: The fabricated compact vector magnetometer achieved a sensitivity of approximately 1.2 nT/√Hz. Although this is not a record sensitivity for diamond-based magnetometers, the device occupies its own niche as a compact hand-held magnetometer.
AI.conclusion: The planar resonator design enables low-power, broadband driving of all four NV orientations, making a compact hand-held vector magnetometer feasible with competitive sensitivity for mobile and geological applications.

title: Quantum extreme learning for forecasting experimental chaotic electronic circuits
summary: Quantum reservoir computing and its special case, quantum extreme learning, are powerful tools for predicting classical discrete time-series with quantum devices. Forecasting continuous signals, however, requires careful discretization as oversampling artificially boosts short-term accuracy but fails over realistic intervals, while undersampling captures too few features and yields poor predictions. Here, we experimentally generate four continuous time-series signals from a chaotic electronic circuit for forecasting with quantum extreme learning. Since simplified circuit models do not fully capture real behaviour, it is unclear whether algorithms that predict simulated time-series also work for experimental signals. We address discretization via two approaches: (i) sampling local peaks/troughs; and (ii) uniform sampling at the autocorrelation timescale. The former captures resonant behaviour, while the latter fully captures chaotic features as well as allowing the reconstruction of chaotic attractors. Our algorithm achieves high forecasting accuracy for both simulated and experimental signals, demonstrating its power for continuous signal processing on near-term quantum simulators, and remains robust against moderate decoherence.

AI.tldr: Quantum extreme learning forecasts four continuous chaotic time-series signals from an electronic circuit, using peak/trough sampling and uniform sampling at the autocorrelation timescale to handle discretization, achieving high accuracy on both simulated and experimental signals and robustness to moderate decoherence.
AI.motivation: Quantum reservoir computing and quantum extreme learning predict classical discrete time-series well, but forecasting continuous signals requires careful discretization: oversampling artificially inflates short-term accuracy yet fails over realistic intervals, while undersampling captures too few features and yields poor predictions. Additionally, since simplified circuit models do not fully capture real behavior, it is unclear whether algorithms validated on simulated time-series transfer to experimental signals.
AI.method: The authors experimentally generate four continuous time-series signals from a chaotic electronic circuit for forecasting with quantum extreme learning. They address discretization via two approaches: (i) sampling local peaks/troughs, which captures resonant behavior; and (ii) uniform sampling at the autocorrelation timescale, which fully captures chaotic features and enables reconstruction of chaotic attractors.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves high forecasting accuracy for both simulated and experimental signals, and remains robust against moderate decoherence.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates the power of quantum extreme learning for continuous signal processing on near-term quantum simulators, and its validity on experimental (non-simulated) chaotic signals supports practical applicability despite imperfect circuit models.

title: Modelling Josephson Junctions with Boundary Conditions: Towards High-Fidelity Models for Superconducting Qubits
summary: Josephson junctions are the central nonlinear element of superconducting qubits, yet their standard description is reached through a chain of approximations. We propose a purely quantum-mechanical model of the junction, formulated directly in Hilbert space: a charged particle moves on a one-dimensional loop, and the junction is a point at which the wave function obeys self-adjoint boundary conditions, labelled by a coupling strength $λ$, which controls the transparency of the junction, and a phase jump $δ$, which plays the role of the superconducting phase difference. For a loop with a single junction we solve the spectral problem and show that the ground-state momentum expectation, identified with the supercurrent, factorises exactly as $\langle\hat{p}_0\rangle = I_c(δ,λ)\sinδ$. For opaque junctions $I_c$ becomes independent of $δ$ and the first Josephson relation $I=I_c\sinδ$ is recovered; for strongly attractive coupling, where the ground state is bound to the junction, the $\sinδ$ law is also recovered, but with an exponentially suppressed amplitude. For more transparent junctions, however, the model \emph{predicts} deviations from the pure $\sinδ$ law: $I_c$ acquires a dependence on $δ$ already at order $λ^{-2}$, compatible with the higher Josephson harmonics recently found necessary to describe superconducting qubit spectra, and a fully transparent contact yields a current linear in $δ$. When the phase varies in time, a gauge transformation shows that the voltage drop across the junction is proportional to $\dotδ$, so that the second Josephson relation emerges without being imposed. The boundary-condition approach thus reproduces both Josephson relations from first principles and predicts corrections to them, offering a route towards higher-fidelity models of superconducting qubits.

AI.tldr: A purely quantum-mechanical Hilbert-space model of a Josephson junction, where the junction is a point with self-adjoint boundary conditions labelled by coupling strength λ and phase jump δ, reproduces both Josephson relations from first principles and predicts higher-harmonic corrections relevant to superconducting qubits.
AI.motivation: Josephson junctions are the central nonlinear element of superconducting qubits, but their standard description relies on a chain of approximations. The authors seek a first-principles quantum-mechanical formulation that avoids these approximations and can capture corrections needed for high-fidelity qubit models.
AI.method: A charged particle is placed on a one-dimensional loop representing the junction as a point where the wave function obeys self-adjoint boundary conditions, labelled by a coupling strength λ (junction transparency) and a phase jump δ (superconducting phase difference). The spectral problem is solved for a single-junction loop.
AI.result: The ground-state momentum expectation (supercurrent) factorises exactly as ⟨p̂₀⟩ = I_c(δ,λ) sin δ. For opaque junctions I_c is δ-independent, recovering I = I_c sin δ; for strongly attractive coupling the sin δ law holds with exponentially suppressed amplitude. More transparent junctions show deviations: I_c acquires δ dependence already at order λ⁻², consistent with higher Josephson harmonics, and a fully transparent contact gives a current linear in δ. Time-varying phase yields a voltage proportional to δ̇ via gauge transformation.
AI.conclusion: The boundary-condition approach reproduces both Josephson relations from first principles, including the second relation without imposing it, and predicts corrections to them, offering a route towards higher-fidelity models of superconducting qubits.

title: Harmonic analysis and circuit approximation of Sobolev functions on quantum input spaces
summary: We derive approximation rates for Sobolev functions defined on the complex unit sphere and complex projective space, representing quantum states, and on the special and projective unitary groups, representing quantum unitary operations. By using harmonic analysis on compact groups and compact homogeneous spaces, we characterize the corresponding Peter--Weyl decompositions and Sobolev spaces via irreducible representations and the Laplace--Beltrami operator. Combining spectral truncation with finite-depth quantum-circuit approximation, invoking the Solovay--Kitaev theorem, we establish quantitative rates that separate the spectral truncation error from the circuit approximation error.

AI.tldr: The paper derives quantitative approximation rates for Sobolev functions on the complex unit sphere, complex projective space (quantum states), and the special/projective unitary groups (quantum operations), separating spectral truncation error from quantum-circuit approximation error.
AI.motivation: Approximating functions on spaces representing quantum states and unitary operations is central to quantum computing and quantum information. A principled understanding of how well such functions can be approximated—and how different error sources contribute—is needed for quantitative guarantees.
AI.method: The authors apply harmonic analysis on compact groups and compact homogeneous spaces, characterize Peter–Weyl decompositions and Sobolev spaces via irreducible representations and the Laplace–Beltrami operator, and combine spectral truncation with finite-depth quantum-circuit approximation using the Solovay–Kitaev theorem.
AI.result: Quantitative approximation rates are established that separate the spectral truncation error from the circuit approximation error for Sobolev functions on these spaces.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a rigorous, harmonic-analysis-based account of approximation on quantum-relevant manifolds and groups, with cleanly decomposed error contributions.

title: Finite Quantum Engineering Thermodynamics
summary: A useful thermodynamic model predicts what a device will do without tracking its full microscopic state. For a finite quantum working medium, the difficult question is which quantities should actually be measured. We develop a task-based method that keeps exact energy accounting separate from calibrated macroscopic prediction. Operator geometry identifies what a measured record determines and bounds what remains uncertain. We then compare direct measurements of dynamical observables with earlier measurements of the same coarse record, selecting the representation together with its measurement cost. A Bose--Hubbard example yields a compact response table tested over a continuous operating region and on unseen microscopic trajectories. A driven Ising chain shows why history is not always the cheaper choice. The result is a way to turn detailed quantum dynamics into a small, reusable, and explicitly qualified thermodynamic description.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a task-based method for building compact thermodynamic models of finite quantum working media by separating exact energy accounting from calibrated macroscopic prediction, using operator geometry to bound uncertainty and selecting measurement representations by cost.
AI.motivation: Predicting device behavior without tracking the full microscopic state is desirable, but for finite quantum working media it is unclear which quantities must actually be measured. The challenge is to determine which measured records suffice for reliable thermodynamic prediction and at what measurement cost.
AI.method: A task-based method that separates exact energy accounting from calibrated macroscopic prediction. Operator geometry identifies what a measured record determines and bounds remaining uncertainty. Direct measurements of dynamical observables are compared with earlier measurements of the same coarse record, selecting the representation together with its measurement cost. Validated on a Bose-Hubbard example and a driven Ising chain.
AI.result: The Bose-Hubbard example yields a compact response table tested over a continuous operating region and on unseen microscopic trajectories. The driven Ising chain demonstrates that history is not always the cheaper measurement choice.
AI.conclusion: The method turns detailed quantum dynamics into a small, reusable, and explicitly qualified thermodynamic description, enabling practical prediction for finite quantum working media.

title: Construction of isoscattering non-isospectral quantum graphs using the concept of a germ graph
summary: The recently developed concept of germ graphs (P. Kurasov {\it et al.}, Phys. Rev. Research {\bf 7}, L022071 (2025)) is employed to construct families of isocattering, non-isospectral graphs that exhibit dissipation. More specifically, a new pair of isoscattering non-isospectral graphs is constructed by connecting the existing isoscattering non-isospectral graphs, so called attachments, to the different contact vertices of the germ graph. The existing isoscattering non-isospectral graphs contained a two-loop graph labelled $Γ_{A2}$ and a three-loop graph labelled $Γ_{A3}$. These graphs have an equal total metric length, but different topologies. The resulting graphs $Γ_3$ and $Γ_4$ are verified as non-isospectral using their Euler characteristics, while their isoscattering properties are investigated by calculating the one-port scattering matrices numerically.

AI.tldr: Using germ graphs, the authors construct new isoscattering, non-isospectral graphs with dissipation by attaching existing isoscattering attachments (Γ_A2, Γ_A3) to different contact vertices, verifying non-isospectrality via Euler characteristics and isoscattering via one-port scattering matrices.
AI.motivation: The concept of germ graphs offers a new framework for generating isoscattering, non-isospectral quantum graphs. The paper aims to exploit this concept to systematically build new families of such graphs exhibiting dissipation, extending known isoscattering non-isospectral examples.
AI.method: A new pair of isoscattering non-isospectral graphs (Γ_3 and Γ_4) is constructed by connecting existing isoscattering non-isospectral graphs, called attachments—specifically a two-loop graph Γ_A2 and a three-loop graph Γ_A3 with equal total metric length but different topologies—to different contact vertices of the germ graph. Non-isospectrality is verified using Euler characteristics, and isoscattering properties are investigated by numerically computing the one-port scattering matrices.
AI.result: The resulting graphs Γ_3 and Γ_4 are confirmed to be non-isospectral via their Euler characteristics. Their isoscattering property is demonstrated through numerical calculation of the one-port scattering matrices, establishing them as a new pair of isoscattering non-isospectral graphs with dissipation.
AI.conclusion: The germ graph concept is a productive tool for constructing families of isoscattering, non-isospectral graphs with dissipation. By attaching existing isoscattering non-isospectral graphs to different contact vertices, new members of this class can be generated, as exemplified by Γ_3 and Γ_4.

title: Correlation-Based Measurement of Entanglement in Rank-2 Mixed States
summary: We study correlation-based entanglement evaluation in rank-2 mixed states of two- and multi-qubit systems. The relevant two-dimensional subspace is treated as a logical qubit embedded in the physical Hilbert space, and factorizable realizations of its logical Pauli operators are classified. For two qubits, this yields nontrivial canonical encodings related by local Clifford transformations. The relation between logical and physical Bloch vectors admits a geometric interpretation as a transversely deformed Bloch sphere, leading to closed-form expressions for two-qubit concurrence and generalized concurrence across $N$-qubit bipartitions. The entanglement scaling factor is obtained directly from complementary-subsystem correlations, without prior calibration of state-preparation parameters. Noisy simulations using the IBM Quantum FakeKingston backend model, with readout-error mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation, confirm the analytical results up to $N=10$ qubits. The protocol therefore enables entanglement estimation from only a small number of measurement settings for this class of rank-2 logical states.

AI.tldr: Rank-2 mixed states are treated as logical qubits embedded in physical space; classifying factorizable logical Pauli operators yields canonical encodings, a geometric "deformed Bloch sphere" picture, closed-form concurrence expressions, and a calibration-free entanglement estimation protocol validated on IBM hardware up to 10 qubits.
AI.motivation: Entanglement evaluation typically requires full state tomography or prior calibration of state-preparation parameters. The paper aims to estimate entanglement in rank-2 mixed states of two- and multi-qubit systems directly from correlation measurements, avoiding such overhead.
AI.method: The two-dimensional subspace is modeled as a logical qubit embedded in the physical Hilbert space; factorizable realizations of its logical Pauli operators are classified. For two qubits this gives nontrivial canonical encodings linked by local Clifford transformations. The mapping between logical and physical Bloch vectors is interpreted geometrically as a transversely deformed Bloch sphere. Closed-form expressions for two-qubit concurrence and generalized concurrence across N-qubit bipartitions are derived, with the entanglement scaling factor obtained from complementary-subsystem correlations. Noisy simulations use the IBM Quantum FakeKingston backend with readout-error mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation.
AI.result: Nontrivial canonical encodings of logical Pauli operators for two-qubit rank-2 states, related by local Clifford transformations, are identified. Closed-form concurrence and generalized concurrence formulas are obtained, and the entanglement scaling factor follows directly from complementary-subsystem correlations. Noisy simulations confirm the analytical results up to N=10 qubits, with entanglement estimation achievable from only a few measurement settings.
AI.conclusion: For rank-2 logical states, entanglement can be estimated from a small number of measurement settings without calibrating state-preparation parameters, with analytical predictions confirmed under realistic noise up to 10 qubits.

title: Decoder- and Noise-Aware Optimization Framework for Clifford-Deformed Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
summary: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computing requires qubit-efficient quantum error correction (QEC). Clifford deformations (CDs) modify the stabilizers of a QEC code to lower its logical error rate at no additional resource cost. However, the number of possible CDs grows exponentially with the number of qubits, making exhaustive search infeasible beyond small codes. In this work, we further show that under circuit level noise the optimal CD depends strongly on both the noise model and decoder. To make systematic CD optimization possible, we introduce Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI), a shot-efficient search algorithm that treats the circuit, noise model and decoder as a black box. We benchmark EBBI's performance on the rotated surface code, under two strongly $Z$-biased circuit-level noise models with the PyMatching decoder. At distance 3, EBBI finds the optimal CD using up to $\sim 1100\times$ fewer shots than random search. At distance 5, when run at the target error rate, the median EBBI run converges to the CDs we believe to be optimal, while random search never converges. Under a $Z$-biased SI1000-like noise model, EBBI discovers a new CD, the B-XZZX code, which we generalized to larger distances. It differs from XZZX on only a fraction $\mathcal{O}(d^{-1})$ of the qubits at code distance $d$, yet its relative advantage grows from $\approx 5\%$ at $d = 3$ to $\approx 12\%$ at $d = 11$. We thus show that the B-XZZX pattern found by EBBI can be systematically scaled to larger code distances. Our work represents a first step towards scalable CD optimization for general QEC codes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI), a shot-efficient black-box search algorithm for optimizing Clifford deformations (CDs) in quantum error correction codes, discovering a scalable B-XZZX code with growing advantages at larger distances.
AI.motivation: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computing requires qubit-efficient QEC. Clifford deformations can lower logical error rates at no extra resource cost, but the number of possible CDs grows exponentially with qubit count, making exhaustive search infeasible. Moreover, under circuit-level noise the optimal CD depends strongly on both noise model and decoder, motivating a systematic optimization approach.
AI.method: The authors propose Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI), a shot-efficient search algorithm treating the circuit, noise model, and decoder as a black box. They benchmark it on the rotated surface code under two strongly Z-biased circuit-level noise models with the PyMatching decoder.
AI.result: At distance 3, EBBI finds the optimal CD with up to ~1100x fewer shots than random search. At distance 5, the median EBBI run converges to the believed-optimal CDs while random search never converges. Under a Z-biased SI1000-like noise model, EBBI discovers a new B-XZZX code, generalized to larger distances; it differs from XZZX on only O(d^-1) qubits at distance d, yet its relative advantage grows from ~5% at d=3 to ~12% at d=11.
AI.conclusion: The B-XZZX pattern found by EBBI can be systematically scaled to larger code distances, representing a first step towards scalable CD optimization for general QEC codes.

title: Entanglement Catalysis Beyond the Asymptotic Rate
summary: Quantum entanglement is a fundamental resource in quantum information science, commonly consumed to perform tasks like quantum teleportation and quantum key distribution. Entanglement concentration converts partially entangled pure states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. While its efficiency is well understood in the asymptotic limit, practical protocols must operate with finite systems. In this finite regime, and at the low error levels relevant in practice, performance is penalized by corrections that reduce the achievable yield. We investigate whether this fundamental finite-size penalty can be mitigated by an entanglement catalyst: an auxiliary state that aids the transformation but is returned exactly and uncorrupted. Although such a catalyst cannot increase the leading-order asymptotic yield, we show that it fundamentally alters the finite-size scaling. For every bipartite pure state with nonuniform Schmidt coefficients, we exactly determine the optimal second-order correction to the yield and show that catalysis completely overcomes this finite-size penalty.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an entanglement catalyst can eliminate the second-order finite-size penalty in entanglement concentration for bipartite pure states with nonuniform Schmidt coefficients, even though it cannot improve the leading-order asymptotic yield.
AI.motivation: Entanglement concentration is essential for quantum information tasks, and its asymptotic efficiency is well understood. However, practical protocols operate in the finite-size regime at low error levels, where finite-size corrections reduce the achievable yield. The authors ask whether this fundamental finite-size penalty can be mitigated using an entanglement catalyst.
AI.method: The authors analyze entanglement concentration for bipartite pure states, introducing an auxiliary catalyst state that assists the transformation but is returned exactly and uncorrupted. They compute the optimal second-order correction to the yield for every bipartite pure state with nonuniform Schmidt coefficients and examine how catalysis affects the finite-size scaling.
AI.result: Although the catalyst cannot increase the leading-order asymptotic yield, it fundamentally alters the finite-size scaling: catalysis completely overcomes the finite-size penalty, and the optimal second-order correction to the yield is exactly determined.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement catalysis eliminates the finite-size penalty in entanglement concentration, offering a route to more efficient finite-regime protocols without sacrificing asymptotic optimality.

title: Genuine multipartite nonlocality detection in graph states
summary: Experimental detection of multipartite Bell nonlocality faces many challenges. The increase in the size of the system demands a higher fidelity of state preparation, a higher detection efficiency, and a larger number of correlators that need to be estimated. These issues are even more pronounced if one wishes to detect a more restrictive variant of Bell nonlocality called genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL). In this work, we introduce two classes of multipartite Bell inequalities that are capable of detecting GMNL correlations and address different experimental hurdles in GMNL detection. The first class consists of the number of correlators that scales linearly with the number of parties. The second class increases the number of correlators and, in return, provides higher noise robustness of GMNL detection. Both classes of inequalities are constructed to detect GMNL in graph states, and in fact both can be used for self-testing of graph states and the performed measurements.

AI.tldr: This work introduces two classes of multipartite Bell inequalities for detecting genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) that address different experimental challenges, and both can self-test graph states and measurements.
AI.motivation: Experimental detection of multipartite Bell nonlocality is challenging due to the need for higher state-preparation fidelity, higher detection efficiency, and a growing number of correlators as system size increases. These difficulties are amplified when detecting genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL).
AI.method: Two classes of multipartite Bell inequalities are constructed. The first class uses a number of correlators scaling linearly with the number of parties. The second class uses more correlators but offers higher noise robustness. Both are designed to detect GMNL in graph states.
AI.result: Both classes of inequalities enable GMNL detection in graph states. The first class minimizes correlator count, while the second class trades additional correlators for greater noise robustness.
AI.conclusion: Both classes of inequalities can also be used for self-testing of graph states and the performed measurements, providing practical tools for GMNL detection addressing different experimental hurdles.

title: Operational signatures of exceptional quantum channels
summary: Exceptional points (EPs) are usually introduced as defective degeneracies of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians and, in fully open quantum dynamics, of Liouvillian generators. Here we formulate an operational theory of exceptional points that does not invoke a Hamiltonian or a master equation. The primitive dynamical object is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) quantum channel $Φ$, applied an integer number $n$ of times, while physical data are probabilities $p_n^{\mathbf A}(x|ρ)$ associated with states $ρ$ and observables $\mathbf A$ having measurements results $x$. We define exceptional channels through nontrivial Jordan chains of $Φ$ and show that a Jordan block of order $m$ generates discrete polynomial-exponential terms with maximal degree $m-1$. This places the physics of exceptional points in contact with what can be directly measured in experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an operational, channel-based theory of exceptional points (EPs) that avoids Hamiltonians or master equations, defining exceptional channels via nontrivial Jordan chains of a CPTP map and relating Jordan block order to observable polynomial-exponential dynamics.
AI.motivation: EPs are conventionally defined as defective degeneracies of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians or Liouvillian generators, which ties the concept to specific dynamical equations rather than to directly measurable quantities. The authors seek a formulation of exceptional points that does not invoke a Hamiltonian or a master equation, so that EP physics connects to experimentally accessible data.
AI.method: The primitive dynamical object is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) quantum channel Φ applied n times. Physical data are probabilities p_n^A(x|ρ) associated with states ρ and observables A with measurement results x. Exceptional channels are defined through nontrivial Jordan chains of Φ, and the structure of these chains is analyzed via the Jordan decomposition of the channel.
AI.result: A Jordan block of order m is shown to generate discrete polynomial-exponential terms in the measured probabilities with maximal polynomial degree m−1. Thus the order of the Jordan block—and hence the exceptional point structure—is encoded in observable measurement statistics.
AI.conclusion: Exceptional points can be characterized operationally through measurement probabilities of a CPTP channel, without reference to a Hamiltonian or master equation, placing EP physics in direct contact with what can be measured in experiments.

title: Finite-Size Limits of Adaptive Pauli Prediction
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures; includes 13 pages of Supplemental Material
summary: Can quantum data reliably answer questions chosen from earlier results? We prove that $M$ adaptive Pauli predictions on $n$ qubits require $Ω(\sqrt{\min\{n,M\}})$ copies at fixed accuracy. Published upper bounds make this tight for $M\le n$. Thus $n$ adaptive predictions cost $Θ(\sqrt n)$ copies, whereas a fixed list costs only $O(\log n)$. The lower bound uses diagonal states and commuting observables, identifying a statistical cost of adaptation. We also quantify how this cost increases with precision.

AI.tldr: For $M$ adaptive Pauli predictions on $n$ qubits, $\\Omega(\\sqrt{\\min\\{n,M\\}})$ copies are necessary at fixed accuracy—tight for $M\\le n$, so $n$ adaptive predictions cost $\\Theta(\\sqrt n)$ versus only $O(\\log n)$ for a fixed list.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether quantum data can reliably answer questions chosen adaptively based on earlier results. It aims to identify a fundamental statistical cost of adaptation in quantum prediction tasks, contrasting adaptive prediction against non-adaptive (fixed-list) prediction.
AI.method: The proof establishes a lower bound of $\\Omega(\\sqrt{\\min\\{n,M\\}})$ copies for $M$ adaptive Pauli predictions on $n$ qubits at fixed accuracy. The argument relies on diagonal states and commuting observables, and further quantifies how the cost grows with increasing precision.
AI.result: The lower bound is tight against published upper bounds for $M\\le n$. Consequently, $n$ adaptive predictions require $\\Theta(\\sqrt n)$ copies, whereas answering a fixed list of predictions needs only $O(\\log n)$ copies. The analysis isolates a statistical cost attributable to adaptation and characterizes its increase with precision.
AI.conclusion: Adaptivity in quantum prediction incurs a genuine statistical penalty: choosing questions based on earlier outcomes is fundamentally more costly than committing to a fixed list, with the gap growing from $O(\\log n)$ to $\\Theta(\\sqrt n)$ for $n$ predictions.

title: Judd-Ofelt analysis and coherent spectroscopy of europium-based molecular complexes for quantum information applications
summary: Rare-earth-ion based molecular crystals are emerging as a promising platform for quantum information applications, combining long optical coherence times with the chemical tunability of coordination chemistry. Here we present a comprehensive optical characterisation of twelve Eu$^{3+}$-based molecular complexes, with a focus on the coherent $^{5}\text{D}_{0} \longrightarrow \ ^{7}\text{F}_{0}$ transition at $\sim$580 nm. Judd-Ofelt analyses are performed across all complexes, providing insights into ligand-field environments, local point-group symmetries, and the resulting branching ratios of the coherent transition. We find that lower point-group symmetry (C$_1$, C$_2$) yields higher branching ratios of the $^{5}\text{D}_{0} \longrightarrow \ ^{7}\text{F}_{0}$ transition, exceeding 1\% in several complexes. Optical inhomogeneous linewidths measured at 4.2 K reveal narrow linewidths for some complexes of below ten GHz, indicative of a highly ordered crystalline environment. Optical coherence measurements of one of the complexes, 5-Eu, yields an optical coherence time of $T_{\text{2}}^{\text{opt}} = 2.3~μ\mathrm{s}$ at 4.2 K, comparable to the best-performing molecular systems reported to date. Systematic characterisation and quantitative comparison will be key to find structure-property relations guiding rational design of optimised complexes for quantum information applications.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive optical study of twelve Eu3+ molecular complexes reports that lower point-group symmetry boosts the 5D0→7F0 branching ratio above 1%, with narrow linewidths (<10 GHz) and a 2.3 μs optical coherence time in complex 5-Eu.
AI.motivation: Rare-earth-ion molecular crystals combine long optical coherence times with coordination-chemistry tunability, making them attractive for quantum information, but systematic structure-property data across a family of complexes are lacking.
AI.method: Optical characterisation of twelve Eu3+ molecular complexes focusing on the coherent 5D0→7F0 transition near 580 nm; Judd-Ofelt analysis to probe ligand-field environments, local point-group symmetries, and branching ratios; inhomogeneous linewidth measurements at 4.2 K; optical coherence measurements on complex 5-Eu.
AI.result: Lower point-group symmetry (C1, C2) correlates with higher 5D0→7F0 branching ratios, exceeding 1% in several complexes. Some complexes show inhomogeneous linewidths below 10 GHz at 4.2 K, indicating highly ordered crystalline environments. Complex 5-Eu exhibits an optical coherence time T2opt = 2.3 μs at 4.2 K, comparable to the best molecular systems reported.
AI.conclusion: Systematic characterisation and quantitative comparison are essential for establishing structure-property relations that guide rational design of optimised rare-earth molecular complexes for quantum information applications.

title: QTN-RQNN: Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network
summary: Resource constraints and imperfect quantum operations remain major challenges for quantum machine learning (QML) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, particularly for fault-diagnosis tasks involving imbalanced and heterogeneous data. This work proposes QTN-RQNN, a Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network that integrates tensor-network-inspired nearest-neighbor interactions with recurrent quantum processing. The model sequentially encodes input features while propagating quantum memory across recurrent steps and incorporates QSMOTE for class balancing. QTN-RQNN is evaluated on four heterogeneous fault-diagnosis datasets SPID, CWRUBD, EFDD, and SFDD and compared with QNN, QTN-QNN, and RQNN baselines through classification, ablation, multi-seed, convergence, and quantum-resource analyses. Results show dataset-dependent predictive behavior, indicating that increased quantum architectural complexity does not universally improve classification. On SPID, QTN-RQNN improves the RQNN F1-score from 0.3077 to 0.4516 and ROC-AUC from 0.4485 to 0.6970, while the remaining datasets exhibit different performance-resource trade-offs and sensitivity to recurrent timesteps and circuit depth. Across all datasets, QTN-RQNN reduces the two-qubit-gate count from 32 to 24 per sample relative to RQNN, corresponding to a 25% reduction without increasing the four-qubit requirement; the same relative reduction is obtained for QTN-QNN over QNN. These findings establish QTN-RQNN as a resource-conscious recurrent quantum architecture and highlight the need to jointly consider predictive performance and circuit-resource requirements for near-term quantum fault diagnosis.

AI.tldr: QTN-RQNN, a quantum tensor network-based recurrent quantum neural network with QSMOTE class balancing, is proposed for imbalanced fault diagnosis on NISQ devices; it improves F1 and ROC-AUC on SPID over RQNN and cuts two-qubit gate count by 25%.
AI.motivation: Resource constraints and imperfect quantum operations on NISQ devices hinder QML, especially for fault-diagnosis tasks with imbalanced, heterogeneous data. There is a need for resource-conscious quantum architectures that jointly address predictive performance and circuit cost.
AI.method: QTN-RQNN combines tensor-network-inspired nearest-neighbor interactions with recurrent quantum processing. It sequentially encodes input features, propagates quantum memory across recurrent steps, and applies QSMOTE for class balancing. Evaluation on four heterogeneous fault-diagnosis datasets (SPID, CWRUBD, EFDD, SFDD) against QNN, QTN-QNN, and RQNN baselines via classification, ablation, multi-seed, convergence, and quantum-resource analyses.
AI.result: Performance is dataset-dependent, showing that greater quantum architectural complexity does not universally improve classification. title: Dynamical Lie Algebras for Fixed-Gate Quantum Ansätze

title: Locality-Preparation Time Tradeoffs in Dissipative Quantum Systems
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures in main text; 14 pages, 4 figures in supplemental material
summary: Dissipative state preparation engineers quantum many-body states as steady states of an open-system dynamics. The spatial range of the required dissipation sets both the feasibility of analog implementations and the connectivity and control complexity of digital ones. Yet how this locality quantitatively constrains preparation times remains largely unknown. Here, we establish an exact locality-preparation time relation for quadratic fermionic systems and develop a construction that optimizes the locality of the dissipative dynamics while preserving the target state. Applied to the Kitaev chain, our framework reveals sharply different locality-preparation time tradeoffs in critical and gapped regimes. At criticality, suppressing the algebraic tails of the jump operators necessarily forces the preparation time to grow algebraically with system size. By contrast, both trivial and topological gapped phases admit exponentially localized dissipation with a finite preparation time in the thermodynamic limit. Our results identify when fast dissipative preparation is compatible with local control and when criticality imposes an unavoidable dynamical cost.

AI.tldr: This work derives an exact locality-preparation time relation for quadratic fermionic dissipative state preparation and shows that critical Kitaev chains require algebraically growing preparation times under local dissipation, while gapped phases allow exponentially localized dissipation with finite preparation time.
AI.motivation: Dissipation range determines practical feasibility (analog) and control complexity (digital), but how locality quantitatively constrains preparation time is largely unknown.
AI.method: Establishes an exact locality-preparation time relation for quadratic fermionic systems and constructs a dissipative dynamics that optimizes locality while preserving the target state; applies it to the Kitaev chain.
AI.result: Critical regime: suppressing algebraic tails of jump operators forces preparation time to grow algebraically with system size. Trivial and topological gapped phases: exponentially localized dissipation achieves finite preparation time in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.conclusion: Identifies when fast dissipative preparation is compatible with local control versus when criticality imposes an unavoidable dynamical cost.

title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble of Quantum-Classical Models via Combinatorial Fusion
comment: 12 pages, 4 tables, 6 figures; Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (IEEE Quantum Week 2026/QCE26)
summary: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are highly sensitive to circuit architecture, yet most quantum machine learning pipelines select a single best design and discard the remaining candidates. Using a diversity-aware model selection method, we identify subsets of maximally diverse models and combine them with both score and rank combination. Experiments on four binary classification benchmarks covering different domains demonstrate that CFA-based hybrid classical-quantum fusion consistently outperform the best individual model on every dataset considered with improvements up to 6.03% in accuracy. When comparing with relevant literatures, the CFA framework further achieves superior performance across all four datasets.

title: A Hardware-Native Trapped-Ion Hybrid Qudit-Oscillator Instruction Set
comment: 27 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Submitted to ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing
summary: Scaling trapped-ion processors by adding ions remains challenging. Adding an entangling operation between ions extends universality to a connected register of several qudits. The architecture natively supports both phase-space and sideband instruction sets and is implemented in the open-source framework HybridLane. As a representative application, we reproduce the dissipative vibronic dynamics of a three-chromophore complex previously simulated on a hybrid qubit-oscillator superconducting platform. Moving from a one-qubit-per-state register to a single qudit stores the entire electronic manifold in one ion, so every electronic coupling becomes a local intra-ion transition and the lab-frame Hamiltonian compiles directly into the ISA. Under the stated sequential timing model from a 40Ca+ qudit processor, one Trotter step is projected to run about ten times faster on the qudit, with an average RMSE of approximately 1.1 percent against the published reference.

title: Enhanced analogue quantum computation with a logically-encoded XX gadget
summary: The introduction of two-body XX interactions has been shown to improve the performance of quantum annealing in solving certain combinatorial optimisation problems and would enable the simulation of a broader class of many-body Hamiltonians. Due to experimental constraints, such interactions are typically not natively available on analogue quantum devices. To overcome this limitation we introduce the truss gadget. This is an exact construction that generates two-body XX interactions using only one-body X and Z fields and two-body ZZ interactions which are readily accessible on, for instance, superconducting quantum annealers. We experimentally validate the construction by reproducing the dynamics of a target XX Hamiltonian on a trapped-ion quantum processor. We then apply the gadget to an illustrative set of instances of the weighted maximum-independent-set problem on a superconducting quantum annealer. We empirically determine an approximate thousand-fold improvement in the probability of finding a state close to the ground state for these instances, over implementation without an XX interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "truss gadget," an exact construction that simulates two-body XX interactions using only one-body X and Z fields and two-body ZZ interactions available on standard quantum annealers, validated on trapped-ion and superconducting hardware.
AI.motivation: Two-body XX interactions improve quantum annealing performance on certain combinatorial optimisation problems and enable simulation of broader many-body Hamiltonians, but experimental constraints mean such interactions are typically not natively available on analogue quantum devices. A construction is needed to emulate them on accessible hardware.
