AI.conclusion: The truss gadget provides an exact, hardware-compatible route to emulate two-body XX interactions on analogue quantum devices, delivering substantial performance gains for quantum annealing on relevant combinatorial optimisation problems.

title: No advantage from classical assistance for energy-constrained bosonic dephasing channels
summary: We prove that four capacities of single-mode bosonic dephasing channels coincide under an average photon-number constraint: the unassisted quantum capacity, the unassisted private capacity, the two-way classically assisted quantum capacity, and the two-way public-classically assisted private capacity. The assistance may be interactive: the parties can exchange classical messages between channel uses and choose subsequent inputs based on earlier outcomes. For every finite value of the constraint, their common value is the coherent information optimized over Fock-diagonal input states satisfying the constraint. The proof uses a relative entropy comparison with the completely dephasing channel to derive chain rules for the Rains relative entropy and the relative entropy of entanglement. These chain rules give an upper bound on the rates achievable by adaptive protocols whose mean input photon number is constrained on average over all channel uses. We also show that both chain rules are attained by canonical purifications of finite-energy Fock-diagonal states.

AI.tldr: Four capacities of single-mode bosonic dephasing channels (unassisted quantum, unassisted private, two-way classically assisted quantum, and two-way public-classically assisted private) are proven equal under an average photon-number constraint, with the common value given by the constrained Fock-diagonal coherent information.
AI.motivation: Bosonic dephasing channels are central models in continuous-variable quantum information, yet the relationship among their various capacity notions under experimentally relevant energy constraints was unclear. Establishing whether assistance and interaction boost achievable rates is key to characterizing their ultimate communication capabilities.
AI.method: The authors compare relative entropy to the completely dephasing channel to derive chain rules for the Rains relative entropy and the relative entropy of entanglement. These chain rules yield upper bounds on rates achievable by adaptive protocols whose mean input photon number is constrained on average over channel uses. They further show both chain rules are attained by canonical purifications of finite-energy Fock-diagonal states.
AI.result: All four capacities coincide for every finite value of the average photon-number constraint (any two-way assistance conferring no advantage), and their common value equals the coherent information optimized over Fock-diagonal input states satisfying the constraint.
AI.conclusion: Assistance and adaptivity do not increase the capacities of single-mode bosonic dephasing channels under an average photon-number constraint; the capacities reduce to a single computable quantity, the constrained Fock-diagonal coherent information.

title: GPU-Based Parallel BP Decoding for Quantum LDPC Memory
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) decoding requires reliable corrections and low latency over long syndrome histories. We extend BP-SF, an oscillation-guided belief-propagation (BP) decoder with independent syndrome-flip trials, by introducing windowed and streaming operations. Our CUDA implementation combines disordered-memory retries, sliding windows, correlation-aware graphs, and layered scheduling. Circuit-level simulations test fixed-basis memory and complete logical Pauli-frame recovery. On the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code at physical error rate p = 0.002, parallel BP-SF reduces 99.9th-percentile call latency by a factor of 13.15 relative to an eight-chain Relay-BP GPU baseline on 100,000 matched samples for which every tested method's initial BP stage fails within 80 iterations. Windowed BP-SF maintains a flat logical error rate and nearly constant per-round compute time through 512 rounds, reaching a 17.1-fold speedup over monolithic decoding. In 512-round full-frame streaming decoding with 2.97-ms syndrome arrivals, layered BP-SF on a transformed joint graph with 20 retries reduces 99.9th-percentile correction-release age from 166.29 to 36.25 ms relative to the joint graph with flooding updates and 100 retries. These results connect parallel BP post-processing to lower decoding costs and earlier correction release in streaming quantum memory.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the oscillation-guided BP-SF decoder with windowed and streaming operations and a CUDA implementation, achieving large latency reductions and flat logical error rates for qLDPC circuit-level decoding.
AI.motivation: qLDPC decoding demands reliable corrections with low latency over long syndrome histories, which monolithic and baseline BP decoders handle poorly due to high latency and growing compute time.
AI.method: The authors extend BP-SF (oscillation-guided belief propagation with independent syndrome-flip trials) using windowed and streaming operations. Their CUDA implementation combines disordered-memory retries, sliding windows, correlation-aware graphs, and layered scheduling. Simulations cover fixed-basis memory and complete logical Pauli-frame recovery.

Windowed BP-SF keeps a flat logical error rate and nearly constant per-round compute time through 512 rounds, with a 17.1-fold speedup over monolithic decoding. In 512-round full-frame streaming with 2.97-ms syndrome arrivals, layered BP-SF on a transformed joint graph with 20 retries reduces 99.9th-percentile correction-release age from 166.29 to 36.25 ms versus flooding updates with 100 retries.

title: Bicycle Race: small two-block codes on the Pareto frontier
comment: 59 pages: 18 main text + 20 appendices + 8 references + 13 code tables and supplementary figures after the references. 17 figures, 11 tables. Code database: https://github.com/gideonlsx/bicycle-race
summary: Two-block group-algebra codes are among the simplest quantum LDPC codes, and many of them are translation invariant on a twisted torus, which suits neutral-atom arrays and other platforms with movable qubits. We ask how far they go at small sizes when searched systematically across all groups. To tackle this question, we use a series of algebraic constraints and screens to design a search pipeline capable of enumerating broad and complete swathes of two-block codes on a laptop. With it we census about $10^8$ two-block codes with up to $320$ qubits at check weights five to nine. Several of these censuses are exhaustive, and support complete statements; for instance, the Gross code is, up to equivalence, the only abelian weight-six two-block code with $n \le 200$ to reach $kd^2/n=12$, and the known $[[64,18,8]]$ is the best two-block code by $kd^2/n$ across weights five to nine with $n \le 94$. The censuses are also large enough to give insights into where good codes live - they concentrate in a handful of groups; abelian groups give the best codes at small $n$ and non-abelian groups at large $n$, with the crossover appearing to move out as the check weight grows; and high quality codes become $100$ to $1000$ times rarer per draw from weight six to weights eight and nine. Using the group algebra and the census data to steer a statistical search finds four to fifteen times as many good codes as uniform draws in equal time. Among the codes found are $[[102,20,10]]$ and $[[120,24,10]]$ at check weight nine, which we simulate in noisy syndrome-extraction circuits, and $[[288,16,16]]$, the best weight-six two-block code with $n \le 300$. At check weights seven to nine, our best codes exceed the best published $kd^2/n$ with exact distance at the same check weight in most length bands up to $320$ qubits. All codes are available in a public database.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically searches two-block group-algebra quantum LDPC codes up to 320 qubits with check weights five to nine, censusing ~10^8 codes via an algebraic search pipeline, establishing completeness results (e.g., Gross code uniqueness up to n≤200 at weight six), identifying where good codes concentrate, and finding improved codes such as [[288,16,16]] and [[102,20,10]].

The open question is how far these codes can go at small sizes when searched systematically across all groups.

A census of about 10^8 two-block codes up to 320 qubits at check weights five to nine is performed, with several censuses being exhaustive. The group algebra and census data are then used to steer a statistical search.

Good codes concentrate in a handful of groups; abelian groups give the best codes at small n and non-abelian at large n, with crossover moving out as check weight grows; high-quality codes become 100–1000 times rarer per draw from weight six to weights eight and nine. title: An Annealing-based Quantum Neural Network with Discrete Wavelet Transforms for Enhanced Air Pollution Nowcasting
summary: Air pollution poses a significant threat to public health, exacerbated by the rapid industrialization and urbanization of modern society. While traditional deep learning offers predictive capabilities, recent advancements in quantum machine learning (QML) present a compelling alternative. Here, we introduce a scalable hybrid framework that integrates variational quantum circuits with quantum annealing. Leveraging a neuromorphic quantum computing platform to transcend the qubit limitations of the NISQ era, we model particulate matter (PM$_{2.5}$) dynamics using high-density urban data from the UK. We demonstrate that our Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) exhibit an intrinsic resilience to input volatility, significantly outperforming classical baselines (MLP and LSTM) on raw, high-entropy environmental data. Furthermore, we successfully scaled the model to 172 qubits, observing a synergistic enhancement when coupled with wavelet decomposition that achieves state-of-the-art predictive fidelity. These findings establish a critical benchmark for quantum utility, proving that scalable, neuromorphic quantum machine learning can now address complex, non-linear real-world problems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a scalable hybrid quantum machine learning framework combining variational quantum circuits with quantum annealing on a neuromorphic quantum computing platform to predict urban PM2.5 dynamics, scaling to 172 qubits and outperforming classical MLP and LSTM baselines.
AI.motivation: Air pollution threatens public health amid rapid industrialization and urbanization. Classical deep learning provides prediction but faces limitations with high-entropy, volatile environmental data, motivating exploration of quantum machine learning alternatives that may offer intrinsic robustness and scalability beyond NISQ-era qubit constraints.
AI.method: A hybrid framework integrating variational quantum circuits with quantum annealing is developed, implemented on a neuromorphic quantum computing platform to overcome NISQ qubit limitations. Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) model PM2.5 dynamics using high-density UK urban data, with wavelet decomposition added to enhance performance, scaled up to 172 qubits.
AI.result: QNNs exhibit intrinsic resilience to input volatility, significantly outperforming classical baselines (MLP, LSTM) on raw, high-entropy environmental data. Scaling to 172 qubits with wavelet decomposition yields a synergistic enhancement, achieving state-of-the-art predictive fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a benchmark for quantum utility, demonstrating that scalable neuromorphic quantum machine learning can address complex, non-linear real-world problems such as urban air pollution forecasting.

title: Maximally antiflat fixed-particle-number fermionic states
summary: Fermionic Gaussian states are completely characterized by their two-point correlations, making the covariance matrix a natural reference for quantifying non-Gaussian structure. Motivated by fermionic antiflatness, we study its extremal form for pure number-conserving states and ask which states can be maximally antiflat and how they can be constructed. We show that, at fixed particle number, maximal first antiflatness is equivalent to a completely flat one-body reduced density matrix, and we obtain a complete existence classification together with explicit block and cyclic-orbit constructions of all allowed sectors. We then investigate the structure that appears beyond the covariance level. Maximally antiflat states with identical one-body data can exhibit distinct connected four-point correlations, which we characterize through the four-point Majorana Wick error and, equivalently, the connected two-body reduced density matrix cumulant. We show that this quartic structure is necessarily nonzero and formulate its extremization as a two-body reduced density matrix (2RDM) purity problem. Combining this framework with a Hilbert--Schmidt estimate of Christiansen for truncated two-body correlations, we obtain an upper bound on the connected quartic structure in terms of first antiflatness. Our results establish both a complete characterization of maximal fermionic antiflatness at fixed particle number and a constrained hierarchy linking covariance-level flatness to higher-order non-Gaussian correlations.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes maximal fermionic antiflatness for pure number-conserving states, showing it equals a completely flat one-body reduced density matrix at fixed particle number, provides a full existence classification with explicit constructions, and links covariance-level flatness to nonzero connected four-point (quartic) structure.
AI.motivation: Fermionic Gaussian states are fully described by their two-point correlations, so the covariance matrix is a natural benchmark for non-Gaussianity. Motivated by fermionic antiflatness, the authors seek extremal non-Gaussian pure number-conserving states and ask which states can be maximally antiflat and how to construct them.
AI.method: The authors study first antiflatness at fixed particle number and prove its equivalence to a completely flat one-body reduced density matrix; they derive a complete existence classification and give explicit block and cyclic-orbit constructions for all allowed sectors. They then analyze structure beyond the covariance level via the four-point Majorana Wick error and the connected two-body reduced density matrix cumulant, formulating quartic extremization as a 2RDM purity problem and combining it with a Hilbert--Schmidt estimate of Christiansen for truncated two-body correlations.
AI.result: Maximal first antiflatness is equivalent to a completely flat one-body reduced density matrix at fixed particle number, with a complete existence classification and explicit constructions. Maximally antiflat states sharing identical one-body data can nonetheless have distinct connected four-point correlations; this quartic structure is necessarily nonzero and admits an upper bound in terms of first antiflatness.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a complete characterization of maximal fermionic antiflatness at fixed particle number and a constrained hierarchy connecting covariance-level flatness to higher-order non-Gaussian correlations.

title: Quantum Query Complexity of Maximum Degree and its Generalizations
summary: We study the quantum query complexity of several basic graph problems. 1) We prove a tight $Θ(n^{3/2})$ bound for finding a maximum-out-degree vertex in an $n$-vertex tournament, resolving a conjecture of Mande, Paraashar, and Saurabh [FSTTCS'23]. 2) Using the same proof idea, we give a direct proof that finding a maximum-degree vertex in an $n$-vertex undirected graph requires $Θ(n^{3/2})$ quantum queries, a bound implicit in the work of Apers and Lee [CCC'21]. Both lower bounds above hold even for computing only the maximum degree or maximum out-degree. 3) We also study Maximum $(k,n-k)$-Cut, which asks for the largest cut with one side of size $k$. For every constant $k\geq 1$, we give an $O(n^{2-1/(k+1)})$-query quantum algorithm. 4) We establish a reduction to Maximum $(k,n-k)$-Cut involving $k$-Graph Collision, which asks whether the marked vertices of a known graph contain a $k$-clique. For $k\geq 3$, this yields unconditional lower bounds with exponents strictly larger than $3/2$, showing that this problem is strictly harder than computing maximum degree. Additionally, under a conjecture we propose for $k$-Graph Collision, the reduction yields a lower bound matching our upper bound above.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the quantum query complexity of finding a maximum-out-degree vertex in tournaments with a tight Θ(n^{3/2}) bound, proves a matching direct lower bound for maximum degree in undirected graphs, and studies Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut with new upper and lower bounds via a reduction to k-Graph Collision.
AI.motivation: Quantum query complexity of basic graph problems, especially maximum degree and its variants, had open gaps and conjectures. The authors aim to resolve the conjecture of Mande, Paraashar, and Saurabh on tournament maximum out-degree, to give a direct proof for undirected maximum degree (previously implicit in Apers and Lee), and to advance understanding of constrained cut problems such as Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut.
AI.method: For (1) and (2), a unified proof technique establishing Θ(n^{3/2}) quantum query bounds, with matching lower bounds holding even for computing only the maximum (out-)degree. For (3), an O(n^{2-1/(k+1)})-query quantum algorithm for Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut for every constant k≥1. For (4), a reduction from Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut to k-Graph Collision (deciding whether marked vertices of a known graph contain a k-clique), yielding unconditional lower bounds and a matching bound under a proposed conjecture.
AI.result: 1) Tight Θ(n^{3/2}) bound for maximum-out-degree vertex in tournaments, resolving the conjecture. 2) Direct Θ(n^{3/2}) lower bound for maximum-degree vertex in undirected graphs, matching the implicit Apers–Lee bound. 3) O(n^{2-1/(k+1)}) quantum queries for Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut for constant k≥1. 4) For k≥3, unconditional lower bounds with exponents strictly larger than 3/2, proving Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut is strictly harder than computing maximum degree; under the proposed k-Graph Collision conjecture, a lower bound matching the upper bound.
AI.conclusion: The paper settles open questions on the quantum query complexity of maximum (out-)degree problems, providing tight and direct bounds. It further shows that Maximum (k,n-k)-Cut is strictly harder than maximum degree for k≥3 and nearly or exactly characterizes its complexity via a reduction to k-Graph Collision, contingent on a new conjecture.

title: A scalable sample-based quantum diagonalization solver for general Pauli-sum Hamiltonians
summary: A scalable ground-state solver to be used in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) is presented. The solver is built on JAX API, and is intended to be run on GPU platforms and possibly many-GPU high-performance computing facilities. It is capable of subspace diagonalization in up to $2^{30}$-dimensional subspace, with possible upgrades to enable even larger-scale operations. The two main components, a general-purpose eigensolver and an SQD-specific matrix-vector operation function, are described in detail. Efficiency of the eigensolver with respect to the GPU memory is demonstrated using a simple physics model. Furthermore, good strong scaling of the eigensolver in many-GPU environment is observed.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a GPU-oriented, JAX-based scalable ground-state solver for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), capable of subspace diagonalization up to 2^30 dimensions, and demonstrates its GPU-memory efficiency and strong many-GPU scaling.
AI.motivation: Sample-based quantum diagonalization requires diagonalizing increasingly large subspaces, which demands scalable solvers that can exploit modern GPU platforms and many-GPU high-performance computing facilities. Existing solvers are insufficient for such large-scale subspace operations.
AI.method: The solver is built on the JAX API and targets GPU and many-GPU HPC environments. It comprises two main components: a general-purpose eigensolver and an SQD-specific matrix-vector operation function, both described in detail, with a design allowing possible upgrades for even larger-scale operations.
AI.result: The eigensolver achieves efficient use of GPU memory, as demonstrated on a simple physics model, and exhibits good strong scaling in a many-GPU environment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed JAX-based solver provides a scalable and efficient ground-state solution for SQD, capable of diagonalization in subspaces up to 2^30 dimensions, with demonstrated GPU-memory efficiency and strong many-GPU scaling.

title: A Warped Born Rule Turns an Observer into a Maxwell's Demon
summary: Quantum mechanics seems to be an incredibly delicate theory. Slight alterations to nearly any part of its structure can lead to huge qualitative differences and wildly unphysical predictions. title: An entangling Hubbard quasiparticle collider on a digital quantum processor
summary: Scattering of quasiparticles provides direct access to the interactions that govern strongly correlated systems. In this work, we realize the quasiparticle scattering experiment of the Fermi-Hubbard model on a digital quantum processor by colliding a doublon and a holon in the half-filled chain of 21 sites encoded on 42 qubits of the ibm_boston processor. For the first time, we measure the transmission probability of quasiparticles of the Hubbard model on quantum hardware, which agrees with the Bethe-ansatz scattering matrix without free parameters. Beyond the scattering probabilities, the collision generates entanglement by superposing the transmitted and reflected components, which we infer from the particle-number fluctuation. In sharp contrast, a control collision between two doublons shows neither the interaction dependence nor the number fluctuation, as expected for indistinguishable particles. Our work demonstrates that the ability to create quasiparticles of a chosen flavor on demand and program their motion and interactions makes a digital quantum processor a new experimental toolset for probing the entanglement structure generated by quasiparticle scattering.
